Habibullah Khan being dead his legal heirs: Md. Ayub Khan and others ----- Pre-emptee-Respondent-Petitioners
VS
Md. Amiruzzaman and others ----- Pre-emptor-Appellant-Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
At the instance of the petitioners, the Rule was issued by this Court with the following terms: 
"Let the records of this case be called for and a Rule be issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-2 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 23-11-2017 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Paribesh Adalat, Chattogram in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Appeal No. 72 of 2009 reversing the judgment dated 9-3-2009 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Chattogram in Miscellaneous Case No. 82 of 1985 dismissing the case should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper." 

2. Facts leading to the issuance of the Rule are inter alia that the opposite party No. 1 being pre-emptor instituted Miscellaneous Case (Pre-emption) No. 82 of 1985 before the Court of the learned Munsif now Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Chattogram under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, in short, 'the SAT Act'. The contentions of the petitioners briefly are that the pre-emptee-opposite party No. 5 purchased entire land of the case holding by virtue of Certificate Case No. 17440/60-61 on 18-7-1961 and obtained possession accordingly and later on, transferred 177 decimals of land on 5-7-1984 in favour of the pre-emptor by dint of a registered sale deed and also made over possession to him and thus the pre-emptor became co-sharer of the holding by way of purchase. The pre-emptee-opposite party Nos. 1-4 are strangers in the case holding. They purchased the case land on 3-3-1985 by virtue of a registered deed. The pre-emptor was not aware as to the aforesaid sale deed and after that, being aware as to the sale of the case land on 3-9-1985, he procured the certificate copy of the impugned sale deed on 12-9-1985 and came to know that the opposite party No. 5 transferred the case land to the opposite party Nos. 1-4 and thereafter, instituted aforesaid pre-emption case after observing all the formalities. 

3. Having received the summons, the opposite party Nos. 1-4 entered appearance in the pre-emption case and contested the same by filing a written objection that the pre-emption case is bad for defect of parties and barred by limitation and the pre-emptor did not acquire any title in the case holding by virtue of alleged auction sale. The case of the pre-emptor is not maintainable in its present form and therefore, the same is liable to be dismissed. 

4. The learned Senior Assistant Judge was pleased to formulate the following points for determination: 
i. Whether the pre-emption case is maintainable in its present form? 
ii. Whether the pre-emption case is bad for defect of parties? 
iii. Whether the pre-emptee is co-sharer tenant to the case holding? 
iv. Whether the pre-emptee is entitled to get relief as prayed for? 

5. During trial, both the parties adduced oral and documentary evidence. After conclusion of the trial, the learned Senior Assistant Judge was pleased to dismiss the pre-emption case holding the view that the pre-emption case is bad for defect of parties. Challenging the legality and propriety of the judgment and order of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, the pre-emptor preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 72 of 2009 before the Court of the learned District Judge, Chattogram. After admitting the appeal and observing necessary formalities, the learned District Judge, Chattogram was pleased to transmit the record to the learned Joint District Judge, Poribesh Adalat, Chattogram for disposal of the appeal. Upon hearing, the learned Joint District Judge was pleased to allow the pre-emption case and thereby set-aside the judgment and order of the learned Senior Assistant Judge. Being aggrieved by and highly dissatisfied with the judgment and order of the learned Joint District Judge, the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the aforesaid Rule and stay there with. 

6. Mr. Kamal-ul-Alam, the learned Senior Advocate along with Mr. SM Arif, Mr. Kazi Mohammad Joynal Abedin and Ms. Smrity B. Usha appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the opposite party Nos. 1-4 in Miscellaneous (Pre-emption) Case No. 82 of 1985 by filing a joint written objection categorically pleaded that the pre-emption case is bad for defect of parties as all the co-sharers in the khatian were not made parties and substituted opposite party No. 4(Ka) by filing a separate written objection on 11-9-1997 made specific averment to the said effect by mentioning the names of all the co-sharers of the disputed land, therefore, the pre-emption case is hopelessly bad for defect of parties. 

7. He also submits that the Trial Court, on consideration of the evidence on record categorically, found that all the co-sharer-tenants in the case holding and the heirs of RS, PS and BS recorded owners were not made parties; therefore, the Trial Court rightly dismissed the said pre-emption case. But the Appellate Court without adverting the finding of the Trial Court most illegally and abruptly came to the finding that the pre-emption case is not bad for defect of parties. 

8. He further submits that in order to fill up the lacuna of non-impleadment of all the co-sharers, the pre-emptor filed an application under Order 1 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for addition of parties at the appellate stage, but the Appellate Court was pleased to reject the said petition. Unfortunately, the pre-emptor without seeking any remedy before the higher Court subsequently filed an application under Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 for adding the left out co-sharers as parties in the pre-emption case. The Appellate Court rejected the said petition and the pre-emptor preferred Civil Revision No. 2969 of 2011 before the High Court Division and this Division was pleased to discharge the Rule and after that, the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal was filed before the Appellate Division and the Appellate Division was also pleased to dismiss the same. 

9. He next submits that if the co-sharers in the khatian are not made parties, the pre-emption case under section 96 of the SAT Act will be bad for defect of parties. In support of his contentions, he has referred a plethora of judgment reported in the Cases of Indrajit Kunda and others vs Bijoy Krishna Kunda being dead his heirs Biswajit Kunda and others reported in 7 BLT (AD) (1999) 386 (Para.-12) : 5 BLC (AD) 429 and Sree Biraj Mohan Roy vs Binodini Roy and others reported in 12 BLT (AD) (2004) 111 (Para.-6), Habibur Rahman Bhuiyan (Md.) and others vs Galman Begum and others reported in 64 DLR (AD) (2012) 133 (Para.9-11), Binodini Dasi vs Mati Lai Sikdar and others reported in 21 DLR (HC) (1969) 262 (Para. 6-7), Anwarul Huq vs irqbal Ahmed and others reported in 11 ADC (2014) 181 (Para. 121), Lai Miah (Hajee) vs Nurul Amin and others reported in 57 DLR (AD) (2005) 65 (Para. 18-19), Ranjit Sarker and others vs Sree Sukhendu Bikash Biswas and others reported in 17 BLD (AD) (1997) 58 (Para. 12) : 2 BLC (AD) 100 and Jahanara Begum and others vs Md. Aminul Islam Chowdhury and others reported in 17 BLD (AD) (1997) 195 (Para. 7): 50 DLR (AD) 52. 

10. He also submits that the interrogatories supplied on behalf of the pre-emptor for discovering the names of the co-sharers of the disputed land having not been properly answered, the question of defect of parties cannot be raised is of no legal substance in view of the fact that the pre-emptee-petitioners by an affidavit dated 21-12-1998 duly answered the said interrogatories supplied and the pre-emptor-opposite party No. 1 herein did not raise any objection against the same and did not obtain any order from the concerned Court against the same as required under the provision of order XI Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 against the alleged insufficiency of answer to any interrogatories and in view of the fact that admittedly, the pre-emptor did not implead the co-sharers whose names have been specifically mentioned and pleaded by the pre-emptee-opposite party No. 4 (Ka) in his written objection dated 11-9-1997. 

11. He next submits that the Appellate Court without adverting and reversing the categorical findings of the Trial Court on the question of defect of parties most illegally held that the pre-emption case is not bad for defect of parties and thereby, committed a gross error of law causing a failure of justice. 

12. He further submits that the Appellate Court without adverting the findings of the Trial Court so far it relates to the defect of parties most illegally and abruptly set-aside the finding of the Trial Court, therefore, the impugned judgment and order of the Appellate Court is liable to be turned down to secure the ends of justice. In this respect, he has referred to the cases of Ranjit Sarker and others vs Sree Sukhendu Bikash Biswas and others reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 58 (Para-12) and Jahanara Begum and others vs Md. Aminul Islam Chowdhury and others reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 195 (Para-7). He finally submits that the pre-emption case is hopelessly bad for defect of parties; therefore, the Rule is liable to be made absolute to secure the ends of justice. 

13. Mr. Mansur Habib, the learned Advocate along with Mr. Iqbal Hossain, Ms. Shimul Sultana and Ms. Rebecca Singha appearing on behalf of the opposite parties submits that the Trial Court without considering the facts and circumstances of the case most illegally held that the pre-emption case is bad for defect of parties, but the Appellate Court after considering the facts and circumstances of the case and materials on record specifically reversed the finding of the Trial Court and held that the pre-emption case is not bad for defect of parties. 

14. He also submits that the pre-emptee resisted the pre-emption case by filing a written objection on 11-7-1987 taking legal plea that the pre- emption application is bad for defect of parties without specifically mentioning the names of the persons who are necessary parties, nevertheless, the pre-emptor on 13-9-1988 filed application for interrogatories requesting the pre-emptee to disclose and detail the names of the co-sharers, but the pre-emptee-opposite party replied to the interrogatories simply stating "আপত্তির ১৮ দফার ১৫নং লাইন দেখুন।” 

15. He further submits that there were no other co-sharers in the khatian to be impleaded as opposite parties other than seller and purchaser and moreover, the application for addition of parties was redundant, therefore, it cannot be held that the pre-emption case is bad for defect of parties. He relying upon the facts and circumstances of the case, evidences on record and findings of the Appellate Court submits that there is no other co-sharer in the case khatian to be impleaded as the opposite parties other than seller and, as such, the pre-emption case not bad for defect of parties and there being no finding as to defect of parties, pursuant to the application dated 10-2-2010 for addition of parties and application dated 18-1-2011 for the amendment of the plaint, mere filing of those applications will not come as an aid to arrive any finding of defect of parties unless the defect of parties is apparent on the face of the record. 

16. He next submits that the learned Advocate for the pre-emptee-petitioners who referred to the written statement filed by the opposite party No. 4(ka) stated that certain persons were not impleaded as there is no co-sharer of the auction purchaser Yunus Talukder, therefore, the question of impleading them as party does not arise at all. 

17. He finally submits that the findings of the Appellate Court as alast court of facts is based on evidence on record and there is no misreading, non reading and non-consideration of evidences on record and, as such, the same does not warrant for any interference by this Court; therefore, the Rule is liable to be turned down. 

18. Heard the submissions advanced by the learned Advocates of the petitioners and the opposite parties at length and meaningfully read the materials on record. The convoluted question of law critically embroiled in this case has meticulously been waded through in order to reach a just decision. 

19. The learned Senior Assistant Judge dismissed the pre-emption case mainly on the ground that the pre-emption case is bad for defect of parties. The Appellate Court after delving into the facts and law and considering the evidence on record held that since the pre-emptee-opposite party purchased the case land only mentioning RS Plot of the case holding and all the sharers of the RS Record were made parties. Therefore, the record owners of the BS Survey are not required to be made parties. Since at the time of institution of the case, B.S Survey had not been started, the pre-emptee contended that the impugned deed was not aout and outsale deed, but a deed of disclaimer, therefore, the pre-emption case is not maintainable. But the Appellate Court as a last court of fact thoroughly examined the evidence on record rightly held that all the co-sharers of the R.S holding i.e. case holding were made parties, therefore, there is no necessity to implead the co-sharers of the latest khatian which was prepared after institution of the pre-emption case. In the written objection, the pre-emptee-opposite party Nos. 1-4 under paragraph No. 6 stated to the effect: "প্রার্থীকের মোকদ্দমা পক্ষদোষে সম্পূর্ণরুপে অচল।”

20. And under paragraph No.18, the pre-emptee also stated: "নালিশী খতিয়ানের সমস্ত স্বার্থসংশ্লিষ্ট ব্যক্তিগণকে পক্ষ করা ছাড়া অত্র মোকদ্দমা অচল।”
 
21. But the pre-emptee did not specifically mention in the written objection as to the effect who are the necessary parties. Nevertheless, the pre-emptor filed an application for interrogatories on 13-9-1988. Upon hearing, the petition was allowed and the learned Senior Assistant Judge directed the opposite party to give reply as depicted in the application. The opposite party Nos. 1-4 answered in the interrogatories by way of affidavit with the following words: "আপত্তি ১৮নং দফার ৮ম পৃষ্ঠার লাইন দেখুন।"
 
22. It cannot be denied that there is a specific time limit for filing an application under section 96 of SAT Act. In such an application, all other co-sharers by inheritance are to be made opposite parties, but if any such co-sharer is left out, he cannot be added as opposite party beyond the time limit. In a case, some opposite parties were added one and half year from the date of filing of the application under section 96 of the SAT Act. They were added in accordpnce with the provisions of rule 10 of Order 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, in short 'the CPC'. Then a question arose as to whether the case became barred by time due to the delay in adding those persons as opposite parties. When the matter was ultimately taken to the Appellate Division, the view of the High Court is as to the effect that the application for pre-emption was barred in view of sub-rule (5) of Rule 10 of Order 1 of the CPC was accepted; because admittedly, the persons were made parties after one and half year from the date of filing of the pre-emption case. This view finds support from case reported in 2 MLR (AD) 304. Therefore, the application at the appellate stage to be added some persons as co-sharers is redundant. The contention of the petitioners is that the pre-emptor by filing petition under Order I, rule 10 of the CPC and amendment of the Pre-emption Application admitted the defect of parties cannot be accepted since admission is repugnant to law. 

23. It appears from the record that the pre-emption case started its journey in the year, 1985. The pre-emptee-opposite party Nos. 1-4 filed a written objection on 14-9-1987. In the written objection under paragraph Nos. 6 and 18, they contended that all the co-sharers of the holding were not made parties. The pre-emptor on 13-9-1988 filed an application for interrogatories requesting to supply the names and addresses of the co-sharers of the case holding. On 21-12-1988, the pre-emptee-opposite party Nos. 1-4 answered to the interrogatories without mentioning the names and addresses of any person and thereby the pre-emptees waived their right to defend that the pre-emption case is bad for defect of parties. The opposite party No. 4 along with the pre-emptee-opposite party Nos. 1-3 filed a joint written objection against the pre-emption case on 14-7-1987 and after that, the opposite No. 4, Rabeya Khatun, left this transitory world and after her sad demise, her legal heirs were substituted as opposite party Nos. 4(Ka)-4(Ga) by Order No. 142 dated 31-3-1997. The opposite party No. 4(Ka) entered appearance in the case and by filing another written objection on 11-9-1997 made specific averment therein that all the co-sharers in the khatian were not made parties. Since the pre-emptee No. 4, Rabeya khatun, waived her right to defend as to the issue of joinder of necessary parties. One of the substituted heirs of Rebaya Khatun i.e. the pre-emptee-opposite party No. 4(Ka), Kamal Uddin Khan's further written objection making specific averments to the effect that some persons were not made parties to the pre-emption case is an afterthought attempt to get the pre-emption application dismissed for defect of parties. The substituted legal heirs cannot fill up the lacuna of the original pre-emptee No. 4, Rabeya Khatun. It is a settled principle of law that all objections on the grounds of non-joinder of parties have to be taken at the earliest possible opportunity, if it is not taken shall be deemed, have been waived. It is true that non-joinder of necessary parties in pre-emption case is fatal. The pre-emptee-opposite party has to make clear averments in his pleadings i.e. the written objection that who are necessary parties. Mere general denial or gentleman denial in the written objection shall not if so facto dismiss the pre-emption case on the ground of non-joinder of necessary parties. Since the pre-emptor requested to answer and gave the details of the persons, who are necessary parties, therefore, the defence of the pre-emptees has been struck out to that effect. The consequence of failure of giving answer to the interrogatories has been clearly spelt out under Order 11 Rule 21 of the CPC. In this respect, I am tempted to the ratio decided in the case reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 456 wherein the Apex Court held: 
"A reference to Order 11, Rule 21 indicates that it is in two parts. The first part provides for the liability incurred by the defaulting party which fails to comply with any order to answer the interrogatories etc. and the other part prescribes the penalty for default, and it is that if the defaulting party is the plaintiff, penalty is the dismissal of the suit for, non-prosecution and if a defendant, his defence is to be struck off and be would be placed in the position as if he had not defended. The second part of the rule also provides for a procedure, for enforcing the penalty and it must be on an application of the interrogating party and on such application, the court assumes the jurisdiction to impose the penalty under the rule." 

24. The Trial Court held: 
"সাক্ষ্য জবানবন্ধীকারকদের প্রার্থীক পক্ষীয় ১নং নুরুল আমীন তালুকদার যিনি ইহার প্রার্থীকের আম-মোক্তার হিসেবে প্রার্থীকের পক্ষে সাক্ষ্য প্রদান করেন তিনি তাহার দেওয়া সাক্ষ্যের জেরাতে বলেন যে, প্রতিপক্ষদের চাচাতো ভাইদের তিনি চেনেন, তাহাদের ইহাতে কোন পক্ষ করেন নাই, কারণ তাহাদের পক্ষ করার দরকার নাই। ইউনুস তালুকদারের (৫ নং বিক্রেতা প্রতিপক্ষের) অন্যান্য খরিদ্দারদের ওয়ারিশদের মামলায় প্রয়োজন নাই বলে পক্ষ করেন নাই কিন্তু বাস্তবে তাহাদের পক্ষ করা আবশ্যক। কেননা প্রার্থীক এখানে খরিদসূত্রে শরীক না দাবী করিয়া বর্তমান অগ্রক্রয়ের মোকদ্দমা করিয়াছেন। এক্ষেত্রে অত্র মামলা দায়েরের পূর্বের সকল খরিদ্দারগণকে পক্ষ করা আবশ্যক। এতদপ্রসঙ্গে প্রতিদ্বন্দি প্রতিপক্ষগণ ৫নং বিক্রেতা প্রতিপক্ষ কর্তৃক চিহ্নিত ৪-৩-৮৫ ইং তারিখের ৪১৩৪ নং কবলার জাবেদা নকল প্রদ-খ(১) মতে দাখিলপূর্বক প্রমাণে ব্যবহার করেন যাহা অত্র মামলা দাখিলের পূর্বের কবলা কিন্দ প্রার্থীক উক্ত কবলায় ক্রেতাগণকে তাহার ওয়ারিশগণকে পক্ষ করেন নাই যাহা থেকে প্রতীয়মান হয় অত্র মামলা পক্ষদোষে বারিত। তাছাড়া প্রার্থীক নালিশী খতিয়ানের আর.এস, পি.এস ও বি.এস খতিয়ানের কোন শরীক প্রজা বা শরীক প্রজার ওয়ারিশগণকে পক্ষ করেন নাই, যাহাদের আইন অনুযায়ী পক্ষ করা প্রয়োজন। তদভিন্ন অত্র মামলা পক্ষ দোষে বারিত। সুতরাং সিদ্ধান্ত গৃহীত হইল যে অত্র মামলা পক্ষদোষে বারিত।"

25. The Appellate Court reversed the aforesaid finding with the following observation: 
"প্রতিপক্ষ/রেসপনডেন্ট আরো দাবী করেন যে, প্রার্থীর মোকদ্দমা পক্ষদোষে দুষ্ট। কেননা প্রার্থীক/আপীলকারী আইন অনুযায়ী অনেকেরই পক্ষ করে নাই। কিন্তু নথি পর্যালোচনায় দেখা যায় যে, অত্র মোকদ্দমায় নালিশী দলিল শুধুমাত্র আরএস দাগ উল্লেখ করেই সম্পাদিত এবং প্রার্থীক/আপীলকারী উক্ত দলিলে সকল খরিদ্দারগণসহ স্বার্থ সংশ্লিষ্ট সকলকেই মামলায় পক্ষভুক্ত করিয়াছেন। এখানে উল্লেখ্য যে, নালিশী দলিল সম্পাদনের সময় বিএস জরীপ সম্পন্ন হয় নাই মর্মে দেখা যায়। এই ক্ষেত্রে প্রতিপক্ষ/রেসপনডেন্ট এর দাবীমতে প্রার্থীক/আপীলকারী বিএস খতিয়ানের সকল শরীককে অত্র মোকদ্দমায় পক্ষ করেন নাই এই বক্তব্য বিবেচনায় নেওয়ার কোন আইনগত সুযোগ না থাকায় এবং প্রার্থী/আপীলকারী কাকে মোকদ্দমায় পক্ষ করে নাই সেই বিষয়টি প্রতিপক্ষ/রেসপনডেন্ট সুস্পষ্টভাবে প্রমাণ করিতে ব্যর্থ হওয়ায় অত্র মোকদ্দমাটি পক্ষদোষে দুষ্ট নয় মর্মে সিদ্ধান্ত গ্রহণ করা হইল।"
 
26. The law of evidence occupies a unique position in any legal system. The assertion of substantive rights can only be established by relevant and admissible evidence. The law of evidence inspires the whole practice of law in every field capable of leading to litigation. Cases are probably won and lost more often for reasons of evidential acumen, or the lack of it, than for reasons of any other kinds. Evidence is not only the fiber and fabric of the legal system, but also it is very heart and soul. Neither the Trial Court nor the Appellate Court took into consideration that the pre-emptee's right to defend as to the issue that the pre-emption case is bad for defect of parties have been struck out, since the pre-emptees failed to answer to the question requested by the pre-emptor through the intervention of the Court by way of interrogatories. Accordingly, the pre-emptees are legally precluded from adducing evidence and cross the witnesses of the pre-emptor on that issue at the time of hearing. 

27. On my independent and dispassionate consideration of the materials on record and legal position critically involved in this case, I am constrained to hold the view that the said pre-emption case is not bad for defect of parties and the Trial Court most illegally dismissed the aforesaid pre-emption case as bad for defect of parties. The Appellate Court assigning cogent reason struck down the aforesaid finding and rightly allowed the pre-emption case, therefore, there is no apparent reason to interfere with the same and, as such, the Rule shall fall flat. 

28. In the result, the Rule is discharged, however, without passing any order as to costs. The earlier order of stay granted by this Court thus stands recalled and vacated. 

Let a copy of the judgment with LCRs be transmitted to the Court below at once. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Mozibur Rahman Miah, J : At the instance of the defendant No. 1 in Title Suit No. 371 of 2024, this rule was issued calling upon the opposite-party No. 1 to show cause as to why the order No. 08 dated 25-9-2024, passed by the First Court of learned Joint District Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 371 of 2024, rejecting the application filed for rejection of plaint, should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders be passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

2. The salient facts leading to issuance of the instant rule are: 

3. The present opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff filed the aforesaid suit seeking following reliefs: 
(a) A decree of declaration that the Arbitration Award dated 24-1-2021 (Registered in SIAC Registry of awards as: Award No. 008 of 2024 on 24 January 2024) passed in favour of defendant No. 1 by the Singapore International Arbitration Centre in SIAC Arbitration No. 032 of 2023 is a nullity, void ab in to and not binding upon the plaintiff. 
(b) A decree of permanent injunction restraining the defendant No. 1 from pursuing any claim whatsoever arising out of or in respect of the so-called purported award dated 24-1-2024 (fully described in the schedule below): 
(c) Award of costs of the suit in favour the plaintiff and against the defendant No. 1: and 
(d) All other or further relief or reliefs the plaintiff is entitled to in law and equity. 

4. It has been precisely stated in the plaint that since the defendant No. 1 herein the petitioner, voluntarily submitted to the jurisdiction of the court of Bangladesh and contested the proceedings of Title Suit No. 435 of 2022 and even contested the appeal stemmed there from up to the Appellate Division by waving right to invoke arbitration, so he can not take any step taking resort to any Arbitration tribunal and therefore the award alleged to have obtained by it is a nullity. It has further been stated that, the plaintiff on 1-4- 2024 first came to learn about the alleged award when the defendant-supplier served a copy of the application upon it, filed for rejection of plaint in Title Suit No. 435 of 2022 where the defendant-petitioner stated that, he obtained an award on 1-4-2024 and then filed the suit. 

5. The present petitioner who is the defendant No. 1 entered appearance in the suit and on 28-8-2024 filed an application under Order VII, rule 11(d) read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint basing on the provision of section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and section 42 and 46 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 stating inter alia that, the plaintiff reserved no right to file any suit before an ordinary civil court challenging a 'foreign award' and prayed for dismissing the suit on rejecting the plaint. 

6. However, against that application, the present opposite party No. 1—plaintiff filed a written objection denying all the material averments so made in the application stating, inter alia, that the application filed under Order VII, rule 11 is totally misconceived and the abuses of the process of the court as the same has been filed only to delay the disposal of the suit. It has further been asserted in the written objection that, the suit has been filed for declaration that, the purported foreign award is a nullity and not binding upon the plaintiff and then implementation of the award through filing money execution case after filing of the suit cannot be allowed which has been filed only to circumvent the decree might have been passed in its favour and the application so filed by the defendant No. 1, is liable to be rejected. However, the said application filed by the present petitioner as defendant No. 1 was taken up for hearing by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st court, Dhaka and vide impugned order dated 25-9-2024 rejected the same holding that, the provision of section 42 of the Arbitration Act is not applicable in rejecting a plaint as that provision does not speak to set-aside any foreign award vis-a-vis apart from the grounds provided in section 46 to the Arbitration Act, 2001, the plaintiff has also taken several other grounds in the plaint challenging the foreign award which cannot be adjudicated without taking evidence from the parties to the suit having no scope to reject the plaint. It is at that stage, the defendant No. 1 in the suit filed this revisional application and obtained instant rule. 

7. Mr. Syed Emran Hossain, the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner upon taking us to the revisional application at the very outset submits that, the learned judge of the trial court has misconceived innot taking into account of the fact that, the defendant has rightly obtained a foreign award as per clause 13 of the agreement signed by both the plaintiff and defendant dated 1-7-2022 and since the plaintiff had duly been notified before initiating the arbitration proceedings before the Singapore International Arbitration Center (SIAC) in SIAC Arbitration Case No. 032 of 2023, so there has been no scope to say that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 had no knowledge about the continuation and passing the said award. To supplement the said submission, the learned counsel then contends that, after passing the award, by a foreign tribunal, the plaintiff opposite party have two options either to pray for setting aside the award under the provision of section 24 of International Arbitration Act, 1994 (a statute of the Republic of Singapore) and secondly, challenge the award in the execution case when the award winning party will file for its recognition and enforcement before the District Judge under section 45 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 having no scope to challenge the award by filing a separate suit in an ordinary civil court. To fortify the said submission, the learned counsel then referred the provision of section 42 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and submits that an aggrieved party against whom an award is given can pray for set-aside such award by filing a Miscellaneous Case under that provision in case of domestic Arbitration to the District Judge and that of International Commercial Arbitration in the High Court Division held in Bangladesh where there is not provision to challenge a foreign award under section 42 of the Act which alternatively denotes, there has been implied legal bar to challenge any foreign award under section 42 and therefore the petitioner has rightly filed the application under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure on relying upon the provision provided in section 9 of the Code of Civil procedure. 

8. The learned counsel further contends that since the petitioner has already filed money execution case No. 25 of 2024 on 1-7-2024 before the District Judge, Dhaka for recognition and enforcement of the award, so the plaintiff opposite party has every scope to make its all grievences by filing an application under section 46 of the Arbitration Act but without doing so, the opposite party filed a civil suit challenging a foreign award which is totally bar under the provision of section 42 of the Arbitration Act, 2001. 

9. The learned counsel further contends that, though it is the chief contention of the plaintiff-opposite party that since the petitioner entered appearance in Title Suit No. 435 of 2022 filed by it (plaintiff) for compensation where the petitioner contested an application praying for injunction restraining it (the present petitioner) from receiving the LC value, and the trial court and this Hon'ble court rejected the application against which the opposite party also went to the Appellate Division by filing appeal as well as review where the opposite party got an order of status quo for a certain period of time and the petitioner had every knowledge about all those proceedings so it can not invoke Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure yet for having knowledge ipsofacto does not preclude the petitioner to file the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the learned counsel argued. 

10. To supplement the said submission, the learned counsel further contends that, the reliefs claimed in earlier Title Suit No. 435 of 2007 and that of the subsequent Title Suit No. 371 of 2024 is totally different having No. embargo for the petitioner, to challenge the subsequent suit under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed for setting aside the award petitioner obtained. 

11. The learned counsel by referring to the 'notice of Arbitration' issued by the petitioner dated 8-2-2023 (Annexure -B- to the revisional application) and the reply given their against by the present opposite party dated 27-2-2023 (Annexure-B(1) to the application) also contends that, in that reply the present opposite party has clearly asserted to receive the notice of arbitration having no scope to say that it had no knowledge about the initiation and passing the award. 

12. The learned counsel further contends that, since the present opposite party had ample opportunity either to challenge the award before the tribunal where arbitration was held or to challenge it by filing an application under section 46 of the Act to the District Judge, Dhaka before recognition and enforcement of the award obtained by the present petitioner, so the suit cannot be proceeded with. However, in support of his submission, the learned counsel has placed his reliance in the decision reported in 6 SCOB (2016) AD 54 : 68 DLR (AD) 4 and read out the relevant ratio settled therein. The learned counsel next contends that, though that very ratio has been settled in an award passed by an International Commercial tribunal where a defeating party to the award without taking resort to the provision of section 42 of the Act filed a suit in an ordinary civil court for setting aside the award when their lordships ultimately found that under no circumstances can an award be it passed by a domestic or International commercial tribunal be called in question by filing a suit in a civil court. But the case in hand, rather stands in better footing since the award in question is a foreign one passed by a foreign tribunal and since there has been no provision in section 42 of the Act even to challenge such award, so it turns out that the legislature in a conscious manner put an implied bar to challenge such award passed by a foreign arbitral tribunal by filing a suit in an ordinary civil court and finally prays for making the rule absolute. 

13. Conversely, Mr. Aneek-R-Hoque, along Mr. Md. Ramzan Ali Sikder, the learned counsels appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 vehemently opposes the contention taken by the learned counsel for the petitioner and placed fourfold submissions. At the first instance, the learned counsel submits that apart from what had been set out in section 46 of the Arbitration Act for setting aside an award there have been several grounds taken in the plaint of the suit on which the plaintiff-opposite party can proceed with the suit and therefore the learned judge of the trial court has rightly found the suit can be proceeded with other grounds taken in the plaint. 

14. The learned counsel in his second leg of submission then contends that, since section 42 of the Arbitration Act does not speak about setting aside a foreign award, so the plaintiffs opposite party No. 1 has got no other option but to challenge a foreign award by filing a civil suit for setting aside the same and the plaintiff-opposite party has thus rightly filed a civil suit to that effect. Giving reference to the decision referred by the learned counsel for the petitioner reported in 6 SCOB (2016) AD 54 : 68 DLR (AD) 4, the learned counsel contends that, since that very decision has been passed basing on an award held in this country in an International Commercial Arbitration, so that judgment is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case in particular, in rejecting a plaint. Drawing our attention to the provision of section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure the learned counsel further contends that, since from the plaint it does not show, it is impliedly bar, by any law, so rule 11(d) of order 7 of the Code or Civil Procedure will not be applicable here. Today, the learned counsel by filing a supplementary-counter-affidavit and by annexing a good number of documents tried to impress us that the petitioner had earlier filed similar application (under order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure) in title suit No. 435 of 2022 which was rejected on 29-5-2024 and then filed another application under section 7 and 10 of the Arbitration Act, for staying further proceedings of the said suit which was also rejected on 25-9-2024. Apart from that, it also contested First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 57 of 2023 which stemmed from an order dated 2-10-2022 passed by the trial curt rejecting an application for temporary injunction brought by the present opposite party and even contested the appeal before the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1958 of 2023 which was also disposed of on 24-7-2023 and of 21-1-2024 so in spite of having every knowledge about the award passed in its favour dated 24-1-2024, the petitioner for the first time disclosed such award only when they filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure in Title Suit No. 435 of 2022 and soon after coming to learn about getting such award this plaintiff filed Title suit No. 371 of 2024 on 14-5-2024 and only after that, the petitioner filed Money Execution Case No. 25 of 2024 on 1-7-2024 so considering all these material facts, this Hon'ble Court may discharge the rule. 

15. The learned counsel further contends that, a plaint cannot be rejected merely basing on the statement made in the written statement or an application for rejection of the plaint, rather if on the face of the plaint, if it reveals that the suit is barred by any law, only then a plaint can be rejected and nonetheless from the plaint filed by the present opposite party, it does not show that the suit is barred by any law and therefore the trial court has rightly passed the impugned order. However, in support of his submission, the learned counsel has placed a slew of decisions reported in 44 DLR (AD) 242, 60 DLR 47, 1986 BLD (HC) 357 and 57 DLR (AD) 18. From the decision reported in 44 DLR (AD) 242, the learned counsel wanted to show us that, even if a suit is impliedly barred by law it has to be deduced from the plaint itself which is also absent in the suit filed by the plaintiff as well. On those scores, the learned counsel finally prays for discharging the rule. 

16. Be that as it may, we have considered the submission so advanced by the learned counsel for the parties meticulously, gone through the impugned judgment and order, the document appended thereof with the revisional application and the decision cited at the bar. First of all, we would like to examine the impugned judgment and order through which the learned Joint District Judge rejected the application filed under Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the present petitioner as defendant No. 1. On two distinct counts the said application was rejected firstly, the learned judge found that, in section 42 of the Arbitration Act, there has been no provision to challenge a foreign award secondly, there are several other grounds available in the plaint of the suit apart from the ground provided in section 46 of the Arbitration Act basing on which the suit can be proceeded with and disposed of on evaluating evidences supposed to be adduced and produced by the parties to the suit. However, it would be profitable if we take a glance as to what has been laid down in section 42 of the Arbitration Act which runs as under: 
Application for setting aside the arbitral award — (1) The court may set-aside any arbitral award under this Act other than an award made in an international commercial arbitration on the application of a party within sixty days from the receipt of the award. 
(2) The High Court Division may set-aside any arbitral award made in an international commercial arbitration held in Bangladesh on the application of a party within sixty days from the receipt of the award. 

17. On careful perusal of section 42 we find that there have been two options opened for a defeating party to the award to challenge an award seeking setting aside of the same that is, if an award is passed in an ordinary domestic arbitration to be challenged before a District Judge and an award given in an International Commercial arbitration held in Bangladesh to the High Court Division. So, clearly, there is nothing in section 42 of the Act for setting aside any foreign award held at any tribunal outside of our country. The learned judge of the trial court held that since there has been no provision to challenge a foreign award in section 42 of the Act so the suit can continue. But he despondently failed to comprehend that section 42 is totally silent to challenge a foreign award, so the legislature put an emplied bar in setting aside it under Arbitration Act let alone by filing a fresh suit. So, the alleged assertion taken by the trial court on that simple point clearly exemplifies his lack of legal acumen. It is the contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner that since section 42 of the Act is silent about setting aside a foreign award so it alternatively proves that there has been a legal bar and that bar has to be inferred as of implied bar within the mischief of section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that connection, the learned counsel contends that Order VII, rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure does not provide about implied or express bar rather speaks "barred by law" so the plaint can be rejected under clause (d) of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. We find ample substance to the said submission, because the legislature has rightly and very consciously omitted to challenge a foreign award under section 42 of the Act if not filing a civil suit. 

18. Then again, in an effort to enforce the award granted in favour of the petitioner, it filed a Money Execution Case No. 25 of 2024 on 1-7-2024 before the District Judge, Dhaka under section 45 of the Arbitration Act. Now let us reproduce section 45 of the Act, here for our better understanding: 
Section 45 — Recognition and enforcement of Foreign arbitral awards (বিদেশী নালিসী রোয়েদাদের স্বীকৃতি এবং বাস্তবায়ন)
(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any law for the time being in force, subject to the provisions of section 46-
(a) Any foreign award which would be enforceable shall be treated as binding for all purposes on the persons as between whom it was made, and may accordingly be relied on by any of those persons by way of defence, set of or otherwise in any legal proceedings in Bangladesh. 
(b) a foreign arbitral award shall, on the application being made to it by any party, be enforced by execution by the Court under the Code of Civil Procedure, in the same manner as if it were a decree of the Court. 
(2) An application for the execution of a foreign arbitral award shall be accompanied by — 
(a) the original arbitral award or a copy thereof, duly authenticated in the manner required by the law of the country in which it was mad. 
(b) the original agreement for arbitration or a duly certified copy thereof: and 
(c) such evidence as many be necessary to prove that the award is a foreign award. 

19. From the plain reading of the title of section 45 of the Act, we find that there have been two schemes in that section, that is, a foreign award has to be recognized first and if the award winning party can over come such recognition, then the enforcement of that foreign award will come. We have been informed by the learned counsel for the petitioner that the hearing on recognition of the foreign award has not yet been held and he next submits that, the plaintiff-opposite party has thus ample opportunity to file written objection either against that Money Execution Case or file an application before the executing court invoking the provision of section 46 of the Act where different grounds have been set out for negating the recognition of the award like section 43 of the Act. The said submission has got material substance in the context that section 42 does not provide any provision for setting aside any 'foreign award` so the scope of the plaintiff is now confined only to file an application whatever form in be in the Money Execution Case for not recognizing the award and if the award is not recognized and enforced, the petitioner can then avail the option to prefer appeal under section 48 of the Act. Overall, it turns out that the opposite party has the remedy in section 45 of the Act. 

20. Now let us examine what section 48 of the Act says: 
Appeals—An appeal shall lie from the following orders of the Court to the Appellate Division namely — (a) setting aside or refusing to set-aside an arbitral award under sub-section (1) of section 42  (b) refusing to enforce the arbitral award under section 44. 
(c) refusing to recognize or enforce any foreign arbitral award under section 45. 

21. So from section 48(c) of the Act, we find that if any award is not recognized, the aggrieved party (award winning party) can prefer appeal so there remains clear avenue to the present opposite party to challenge the award before the District Judge not to file a separate suit for that. During the midst of argument, the learned counsel also supplied us the International Arbitration Act, 1994, a statute of Singapore and refers us section 24 thereof where we find, specific procedure is there to set-aside an award given by the arbitral tribunal of that country. Though the learned counsel for the opposite party very robustly asserts that in spite of appearing in both the title suits and in the appeals that went up to the Appellate Division, the petitioner did not disclose about getting the award. At this, the learned counsel for the petitioner, by taking us through annexure 'B' and 'Bl' to the revisional application as well as paragraph No. 49 (at page 50 of Annexure 'C' to the revisional application) then submits that those documents clearly proves that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 has every knowledge about initiating and passing the award by the arbitral tribunal in Singapore. But it is totally immaterial whether the petitioner had disclosed about getting the award in two civil suits still as those very factual aspects is totally immaterial in filing and adjudicating a suit. The learned counsel for the petitioner however robustly asserts that in view of section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the suit initiated by the opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff is impliedly bar. For that obvious reason, we feel it expedient to reproduce section 9 here as well: 
Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure 
The Courts shall (subject to the provisions herein contained) have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred. 

22. Since in the four corner of the Arbitration Act, 2001 there has been no express bar to file a suit challenging any award given by a domestic tribunal in an ordinary Arbitration or International commercial Arbitration let alone any award of a foreign tribunal so, filing a civil suit for setting aside an award will definitely be regarded as implied bar as has been stated above. That very proposition has already been settled in the decision by our Appellate Division in a case reported in 6 SCOB (2016) AD 54 : 68 DLR (AD) 4. Their lordships amongst others held that: 
"The Act, 2001 is special law and it has been enacted with the sole purpose of resolving the dispute between the parties through arbitration and after an award is given by the Arbitration, if it is allowed to be challenged in a civil suit, then the arbitration proceeding shall become a mockery and the whole purpose of the arbitration scheme as envisaged in the Act, 2001 shall fail. Therefore the trial court rightly rejected the plaint." 

23. The said decision is squarely applicable in the fact and circumstances of the instant case because when a domestic award cannot be challenged by filing a civil suit then no question can at all arise to challenge a foreign award in an ordinary civil court. On top of that, in our country, a District Judge is the highest seat of judiciary in our subordinate judiciary who has been assigned with the ordinary jurisdiction in all sorts of arbitral dispute save for International commercial dispute. An award given by a tribunal even comprising any former Hon'ble Chief Justice of Bangladesh is subject to challenge before a District Judge under section 42 and 43 of the Arbitration Act. Now if an avenue is opened to challenge an award let alone a foreign award to a Joint District Judge, subordinate to District Judge, it would be a mockery for establishing Arbitration Tribunal if not their award and for that obvious reason, it has been set at rest once for all in the decision by our Appellate Division in 6 SCOB (2016) AD 54 : 68 DLR (AD) 4. 

24. At this, the learned counsel for the opposite party has vehemently submits that, since there has been bar in section 42 of the Act vis-a-vis on the face of the plaint to challenge an award so the plaint cannot be rejected. But from the foregoing discussion and observation, it is now crystal clear that everything needs not be disclosed in a statute which some time has to be deduced from the scheme of a certain statute. Last but not the least, though the learned counsel for the opposite party No. 1 has referred a slew of decisions even passed by our Appellate Division but the facts so have been described in those very decisions is totally distinguishable with the facts and circumstances of the instant case because the award is given in view of an agreed agreement by the parties which can well be amenable under Arbitration Act, 2001 but those have totally been absent in all the decisions cited by the learned counsel for the opposite party No. 1 rather the decision cited and reported in 6 SCOB (2016) AD 54 : 68 DLR (AD) 4 can be taken as a milestone to be followed by us not to challenge an award to any ordinary civil court. Though in the application so filed under Order VII, rule 11 (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, we find in paragraph No. 8, that the learned Advocate before the trial court has also referred the said decision by our Appellate Division but the learned Joint District Judge even did not bother to take into account of the decision and very abruptly passed a judgment giving two absurd reasoning, which is totally beyond the scheme of law and thus the learned Joint District Judge is hereby cautioned not to venture into such kinds of misdoing in future when a judgment of his apex court will be placed. 

25. Regard being had to the above facts and circumstances we are of the view that, the learned judge of the trial court has very mis-concievely and callously passed the impugned judgment and order which can in no way be sustained. 

26. Accordingly, the rule is made absolute however without any order as to costs. 

27. The impugned order No. 08 dated 25-9-2024, passed by the First Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 371 of 2024 is thus set-aside. 

28. Consequently, the plaint of Title Suit No. 371 of 2024 is hereby rejected resultantly, Title suit 371 of 2024 is dismissed. 

Let a copy of this order be transmitted to the court concerned forthwith. 

End.

Mr. Md. Rafiqul Islam Faruk, with Mr. Choudhury Murshed Kamal Tipu, Advocate ------ For the appellants.
Mr. Manzill Murshid, Senior Advocate with Mr. Sanjoy Mandal, Advocate ------ For the respondent no. 1.
parties:
Lokus and another ------ Defendants-Appellants.
