Government of Bangladesh and others -------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Sashanka Shekhar Sarkar, J: This rule Nisi was issued at the instance of the petitioner on an application under Article 102 of the Constitution in the following terms: — 
"Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the directive issued by respondent vide Memo No. 2 ১০.২৮.০০.০০০০.০৩০.১৪.০১৪.২৩.৪৯১ dated 26-6-2024 purportedly under the provisions of বিদ্যুৎ ও জ্বালানীর দ্রুত সরবরাহ বৃদ্ধি (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০১০ instructing respondent No.3 to terminate the Contract of Jet A-1 Pipeline Project with respondent No.4 (Annexure-G) should not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

2. At the time of the issuance of the rule, the operation of the impugned Memo dated 26-6-2024, as evident from Annexure-G to the writ petition, was stayed for 6(six) months from the date. 

3. During the pendency of the rule, the petitioner came up with an application for the issuance of a supplementary rule. Accordingly, after hearing the petitioner on 17-10-2024, a supplementary rule was issued in the following terms: — 
"Let a supplementary Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the notice of termination dated 30-6-2024 issued by the respondent No. 3 BPC hearing reference No. 28.03.0000.055.55.001.24/DLO/317 terminating BPC's contract agreement dated 8-11-2017 and revised contract agreement dated 27-4-2022 with respondent No. 4 NKFTCL (Annexure-L) should not be declared to have been issued with out lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

4. Facts for the disposal of the rule are as stated in the writ petition:—
The petitioner is a joint venture entity formed under a joint venture agreement dated 7-11-2017 between China Machinery Engineering & Construction Corporation (CMECC) and BARAKA Engineers Ltd. (BEL). The JV agreement was later amended by two addenda. The first addendum was signed on 10-11-2019, and the second on 25-11-2021. According to Clause 1 of the second addendum to the Joint Venture Agreement of CMECC and BEL dated 25-11-2021, BEL became the leading partner of the CMECC-BEL (JV) agreement. 

5. The respondent No.1-Government decided to appoint Nou Kollan Foundation Trading Company Limited (NKFTCL) (herein, respondent No. 4) as the Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) contractor by their resolution dated 9-27-2017 for a project called Jet A-1 Pipeline from Pitalganj (near Kanchon Bridge) to Kurimitola Aviation Depot (KAD), including the Pumping Facility Project (hereinafter referred to as "Project"), through the Direct Procurement Method (DPM) under বিদ্যুৎ ও জ্বালানীর দ্রুত সরবরাহ বৃদ্ধি (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০১০. The decision was communicated to respondent No. 3, the Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation (hereinafter referred to as BPC), by respondent No. 1, the Ministry, on 10-9-2017. The purpose of the Pipeline Project was to reduce time and transportation costs for carrying fuel by aircraft from Narayanganj to Dhaka. Subsequently, on 11-10-2017, the respondent No. 3 issued a Notification of Award in favour of the respondent No.4 and proceeded accordingly. 

6. Subsequently, the respondent No.4, after having received Notification of Award from the respondent No.3, engaged China Machinery Engineering and Construction Corporation (hereinafter referred to as "CMECC"), a Chinese state-owned international engineering contractor company and a subsidiary of China General Technology Group, for engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) works of the Project. The CMECC, for completion of the Project, entered into a joint venture (JV) agreement with BARAKA Engineers Ltd. (BEL) (hereinafter referred to as the 'JV Agreement') on 7-11-2017. Subsequently, they operated jointly under the name CMECC-BEL JV- the Petitioner. 

7. That after having received the Notification of Award from the respondent No.3, the respondent No. 4 communicated the letter of acceptance of the Notification of Award to the petitioner on 12-10-2017, and in response, the petitioner vide its letter dated 12-10-2017, addressed to the respondent No.4, accepted the notification of award. Thereafter, the respondent No.4 entered into a joint contract agreement with the petitioner for the completion of the project on 9-11-2017. As per Clause 1(b) and Clause 1(e) of the Joint Contract Agreement dated 9-11-2017, the initial time frame for completion of the project was 9-11-2018, accompanied by a Project cost of BDT 183,33,81,644.77/4. Subsequently, a revised deed of agreement was executed between the respondent No. 4 and the petitioner on 11-5-2022. According to the said revised deed of agreement, the project was rescheduled to be completed on or before 31st December 2022, and the revised budget amount was Taka 267,47,09,221.50. 

8. Following the signing and execution of the revised deed of agreement dated 11-5-2022, as per Clause 4.2 of the General Conditions of Contract, the Petitioner furnished two performance securities in the form of Bank Guarantees initially for Taka 18,33,38,165 bearing No.1103190063 dated 11-4-2019 and subsequently for Taka 8,41,32,758 bearing No.1103220067 dated 26-4-2022 both issued by Modhumoti Bank Limited Gulshan Branch in favour of the respondent No. 3. The said bank guarantees was extended time to time and eventualy it was extended up to 31-12-2024 for this project at the request of the respondent No.4 as evident from their letter dated 5-6-2024. 

9. That at the time of revising the Last Budget, the respondent No.3 over looked potential challenges that could escalate project costs. These challenges include complexities in laying and crossing pipelines across water bodies, canals, railway tracks, inter-district highways, and the Fast Dhaka Elevated Expressway. Moreover, unexpected obstacles such as buried culverts from previous water passages, fiber cables, and various pipelines (water, sewerage, and gas) were not adequately considered during budget planning. Consequently, the revised budget was insufficient. 

10. The respondent No.3, BPC, further revised the project completion timeline to December 31, 2022, following a revised joint agreement dated 11-5-2022. However, this timeline was deemed unrealistic and poorly reasoned. Firstly, the respondent No. 3 spent considerable time revising the budget and project schedule, only to propose an impractical deadline. Secondly, the respondent No. 3 failed to acknowledge its or the Government's shortcomings in acquiring project land for the depot and suitable locations for the jetty along the Sitalaksha River. Furthermore, the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted the project by causing many employees, laborers, and engineers to leave and return to their home countries, resulting in significant delays. Reinstating these workers and resuming project operations required considerable time. 

11. The petitioner exercised diligent efforts to complete the Project, irrespective of the aforementioned difficulties. The impediments impeding the Project's completion were entirely outside the petitioner's control. Notably, the budget allocated for the project, as discussed above, fell far short of the actual expenses incurred and to be incurred, further complicating the execution of the remaining tasks. Moreover, the petitioner was confronted with a series of unforeseeable difficulties, including the unprecedented global disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the geopolitical instability arising from the Ukraine-Russia war. This geopolitical instability has caused a noteworthy fluctuation in the conversion rate of the United States Dollar (USD) against the Bangladeshi Taka (BDT). Before the commencement of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the USD to BDT exchange rate stood at BDT 85. Presently, however, this exchange rate has surged to BDT 120, reflecting a considerable depreciation of approximately 30% in the value of the BDT against the USD due to the ongoing conflict. Asaresult, overseas procurement became costlier. 

12. These adverse circumstances have substantially hindered the petitioner's ability to carry out their obligations. In light of these extenuating factors, due consideration must be given to the petitioner's efforts and the impediments they have encountered. The successful completion of these tasks underscores the petitioner's capability and dedication to fulfilling their contractual obligations to the best of their abilities. The petitioner has already purchased and shipped out certain project-related equipment. All the equipment has been kept in the warehouse for a long time. The petitioner cannot use this equipment in the Project because of a budget shortage. 

13. The petitioner informed the respondent Nos.3 and 4 regarding the aforesaid impediments through letters served by its lead partner, BEL dated 20-11-2023, 4-7-2023, 23-3-2023, 6-11-2022, 4-9-2022, 27-9-2022, 19-9-2022, and 1-4-2024. However, despite the petitioner's correspondence, the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 failed to take any action to revise the Project's budget and timeline, resulting in the Project in a standstill. With the Project currently halted and both the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 having ceased all communication with the petitioner, huge potential financial losses and risks are anticipated on the part of the petitioner. 

14. Despite the petitioner's regular attempts to communicate, respondent Nos. 3 and 4 have maintained silence and have taken no formal measures to communicate with the petitioner to address the lack of clarity regarding the project. This lack of communication has resulted in the petitioner being left uninformed and excluded from any decision-making processes. Subsequently, no project work has been carried out in the year 2023, and the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 have not initiated any measures to address or progress the project forward. Consequently, the Project works have come to a standstill, creating a state of uncertainty regarding its completion. The petitioner perceives this silence and inaction from the respondents as deliberate disregard and exclusion. 

15. The petitioner was apprehensive that the respondent No.3 might encash the bank guarantees numbered 1103190063 dated 11-4-2019 and 1103220067 dated 26-4-2022 at any time. As such, the petitioner filed Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 33 of 2024 under section 7(A) of the Arbitration Act, 2001, before the learned District Judge, Dhaka, seeking an injunction to restrain the opposite parties from encashing the performance guarantees. The learned District judge, Dhaka, admitted the case on 23-4-2024 but did not issue interim order, instead giving the opposite parties a 15-day show cause notice. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the order dated 23-4-2024, the Petitioner filed Civil Revision No. 1839 of 2024 before the Hon'ble High Court Division. The High Court Division subsequently passed an order of status quo for two months regarding the Performance Guarantees. The petitioner also served a Notice of Arbitration on respondent Nos. 4 and 6 on 27-6-2024. 

16. Despite the ongoing silence and inaction of the respondent Nos.3 and 4 in informing any update on the Project to the petitioner, respondent No. 2-concerned Ministry, issued a directive vide its Memo No. 28.00.0000.000.14.014.23.491 dated 26-6-2024 (impugned notice), directing the respondent No. 3 to cancel the Contract of JetA-1 Pipeline Project with the respondent No.4, NKFTCL. Respondent No. 2, while issuing the impugned notice, referred to a letter issued by BPC vide Memo No.28.03.0000.055.55.001.24/DN0/245 dated 28-5-2024. BPC's letter dated 28-5-2024 is the basis upon which the impugned letter was issued by Respondent No. 2 the concerned Ministry. However, BPC's letter does not make any specific reference or allegations as to how the petitioner, orasamatter of fact, the respondent No.4, NKFTCL, was in breach of the contract. BPC's letter refers to the same discussions relating to expansion of budget and time line as has been requested by the petitioner over the last one and half years and therefore, the decision of respondent No.2 asking the respondent No.3 to cancel its contract with the respondent No.4 is arbitrary and mala fide as it has been issued to including a particular 'third-party' contractor instead of the petitioner. 

17. The petitioner is hereby directly aggrieved by the issuance of the aforesaid directive inasmuch as the termination of the contract with the respondent No.4 will result in the petitioner's removal from the Project. Such action would frustrate all the project work undertaken by the petitioner, including encashment of performance security furnished by them in favour of the respondent No.3 as mentioned in the directive. 

18. The respondent No. 2 invoked RIP, বিদ্যুৎ ও জ্বালানীর দ্রুত সরবরাহ বৃদ্ধি (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০১০ in directing the respondent No.3 (BPC) to cancel the contract with the respondent No.4, NKFTCL. However, the Act of 2010 does not contain any provision which empowers Government/Ministry to cancel a contract, substantial performance of which has already been carried out. Infact, sections 5 to 7 of the Act of 2010 clearly manifest that a technical processing committee has to be formed to submit proposal regarding “ক্রয় এবং বিনিয়োগ পরিকল্পনা বা প্রস্তাব” which would eventually be submitted before অর্থনৈতিক বিষয় বা সরকারি ক্রয় সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিসভা কমিটি for approval. In the instant case (as evident from the impugned notice) neither any technical processing committee was formed nor any proposal was submitted before the অর্থনৈতিক বিষয় বা সরকারি ক্রয় সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিসভা কমিটি nor there has been any approval from অর্থনৈতিক বিষয় বা সরকারি ক্রয় সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিসভা কমিটি recommending cancellation of the project contract. 

19. Being aggrieved by, and dissatisfied with the impugned directive dated 26-6-2024 issued by the respondent No.2 purported under the provisions of বিদ্যুৎ ও জ্বালানীর দ্রুত সরবরাহ বৃদ্ধি (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০১০ to terminate the contract of Jet A-1 Pipeline Project with the respondent No.4 (Annexure-G to the writ petition) and the notice of termination dated 30-6-2024 issued by the respondent No.3 terminating BPC's contract agreement dated 8-11-2017 and revised contract agreement dated 27-4-2022 with respondent No.4 NKFTCL (Annexure-L to the writ petition) and there being no other adequate, speedy, efficacious, and alternative remedy, the petitioner has filed the instant application under Article 102 of the Constitution and obtained the present Rule Nisi and an order of stay the Annexure-G to the writ petition. 

20. Facts as stated in the affidavits-in-opposition filed by the respondent Nos.1 and 3, respectively:— 
The respondent No. 3 under took the construction project of building fuel pipelines from Pitalganj, Narayangaj, for the supply of jet fuel to the Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (3rd terminal) from its funds. The respondent No.3 entered into an EPC (Engineering Procurement Construction) Contract with the Bangladesh Navy dated 8-11-2017, requiring the Bangladesh Navy to construct the pipeline. The timeline for completion of the Project was 7-11-2018. The cost of the Project was fixed at Taka 183,33,81,644.77. Bangladesh Navy chose to implement the construction contract through one of its registered company named Nou Kollan Foundation Trading Company Limited which has been impleaded as respondent No.4. Respondent No.3 also appointed the respondent No.5 (Padma Oil Company Limited) as the project manager and Dorsch Holding GmbH, Germany in Association with Dorsch Consult (India) Private Ltd. India ("Dorsch") as the Project Management Consultant ("PMC"). 

21. Subsequently, the respondent No.4 engaged the petitioner as a sub-contractor to carry out some parts of the construction work by entering into a separate agreement dated 9-11-2017 (Annexure-D to the writ petition) executed between the respondent No.4 and the petitioner. The respondent No.4, due to its failure of its sub-contractor, could not complete and deliver the Project work within the agreed timeline (i.e., 7-11-2018). Subsequently, the Project completion time line was extended upto 30-9-2020. However, despite the extension of time, the progress of the Project work was extremely slow, and accordingly, the respondents Nos.3 and 5 had to regularly issue numerous letters, including letters dated 20-2-2020, requesting for speeding up of the work progress. 

22. That in order to provide another opportunity, the respondent No.3 executed a revised contract agreement with the respondent No.4 on 27-4-2022 ("Revised Contract"), under which, the Project price was increased from Taka 183,33,81,644.77 by 44.32% (i.e., Taka 81.28 crore) to Taka 267,47,09,221.50 and new completion timeline had fixed till 31-12-2022. The completion timeline was eventually extended by four years. 

23. Despite the extension of the timeline and anincrease in contractual price, the respondent No.4 was unable to complete the work due to the non-cooperation of its subcontractors. Accordingly, the respondent No.3 and the respondent No.5 had to again issue letters, including a letter dated 22-8-2022, for speeding up the progress of the Project work. That the alleged reasons for delay in completion provided by the writ petitioner in paragraph Nos. 11, 12, and 13 of the writ petition are wholly incorrect and denied by the respondent No.3. The actual reasons for the delay are, among others, as follows. Firstly, the respondent No.3 learnt from respondent No.4 that the petitioner failed/refused to complete every part of the construction of the Project as perits submitted work schedule. By showing various unreasonable excuses, it refrained from opening L/Cs required for the procurement of overseas equipment, presenting designs and drawings before the PMC, laying the remaining pipeline, completing and even commencing the construction of other important items like the depot, control room, sub-station, warehouse, pump, tanker loading, etc. Secondly, the land required for the construction of the depot and jetty was acquired by the respondent No.3 on 2-10-2018. The petitioner failed to commence work on time and submitted defective designs and drawing's due to its lack of skill, which, when submitted by respondent No.4 these defective designs were not accepted by PMC. In response to the petitioner's request based on its submitted designs and drawings, an additional 6 katha of land was handed over to them for the jetty on the specified date in 2021, and subsequently, the acquisition work was completed on the same date in 2021. The construction of the jetty was never commenced by the petitioner despite the handover of the land in the year 2021. Thirdly, the procurement of overseas equipment was scheduled to be purchased within 6-10-2020, but upon failure on the part of the petitioner to acquire so, the sametime line was extended again up to 25-3-2022. However, the petitioner failed again to procure all the equipment within time. Timely delivery of equipment was crucial for the successful implementation of the project; however, the writ petitioner's lack of skill created significant shortcomings in this regard. Out of the 56 pieces of equipment required for the project's execution, the sub-contractor has only supplied 14 items to date. Consequently, the writ petitioner's dilly-dally approach to procure within time was done in bad faith, which was the reason for the delay of procurement, and any price hike is the responsibility of the petitioner. 

24. The tables that the petitioner provided in paragraphs Nos.14 and 15 are a deliberately incomplete description of the Project work. It omitted to mention that only 14 out of 56 items were procured, and the majority of the equipment was not procured by the petitioner within a fixed timeline. The respondent No.4, as a contractor, could not complete the Project work due to the lack of cooperation by its appointed subcontractor, i.e., the petitioner. Furthermore, it also transpires that the writ petitioner subsequently entered into a partnership agreement dated 12-2-2023 (Annexure-8 to the affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent No.3) with another contractor, Buildstone Construction Company Limited ("BCCL"), admitting that it is notin a position to implement the work of the Project. The said agreement further states that the petitioner would only receive the amount from the respondent No.4 for the work so far completed by it, but would not be entitled to receive any amount for completion of the remaining Project work by BCCL. Hence, it readily agreed to the aforesaid arrangement, and hence, its anticipated losses as put forward in paragraph No.17 of the writ petition are designed to harass the respondent No.3 to gain further financial advantage. This also proves that the petitioner has no locus standi to issue the impugned notices, as it has surrendered the work to another private party by waiving all claims to future works (ifany). The petitioner is not entitled to blow hot and cold at the same time. 

25. The respondent No.3 in its letter dated 28-5-2024 stated that the respondent No.4 is reliant on its sub-contractor, and the respondent No.4 failed to complete the Project due to its sub-contractor's professional incapacity and incompetence. After evaluating the whole context, the respondent No. 3 finally took the decision to terminate the Contract with the respondent No.4 by issuing a letter of termination dated 30-6-2024. Upon termination of the said Contract, the respondent No.4 issued a letter dated 30-6-2024 requesting the respondent No.3 to take over possession of the Project site. Subsequently, the respondent No.4 also terminated the contract with the petitioner by a letter dated 3-7-2024. 

26. Mr. Ahsanul Karim, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that respondent No.2 invoked বিদ্যুৎ ও জ্বালানীর দ্রুত সরবরাহ বৃদ্ধি (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০১০ in directing BPC to cancel the contract with NKFTCL; however, the Act of 2010 does not contain any provision which empowers the Government or a statutory corporation such as BPC to cancel a contract, substantial performance of which has already been carried out. Infact, sections 5 to 7 of the Act of 2010 clearly manifest that a technical processing committee has to be formed to submit a proposal regarding “ক্রয় এবং বিনিয়োগ পরিকল্পনা বা প্রস্তাব” which would eventually be submitted before অর্থনৈতিক বিষয় বা সরকারি ক্রয় সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিসভা কমিটি for approval. In the instant case, as evident from the impugned .notice dated 26-6-2024 neither any technical processing committee was formed nor any proposal was submitted before the অর্থনৈতিক বিষয় বা সরকারি ক্রয় সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিসভা কমিটি nor there has been any approval from অর্থনৈতিক বিষয় বা সরকারি ক্রয় সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিসভা কমিটি recommending cancellation of the project contract. 

27. Mr. Karim further submits that it is a settled principle of law that if a vested right of a person is to be taken away, he must be given an opportunity of being heard before passing any order affecting his right. The impugned notice directive 26-6-2024 and the BPC letter dated 28-5-2024 indicate that neither a show cause notice nor any prior notification was issued to the petitioner or the respondent No.4, asking any explanation. It appears that BPC was aware all along of the project's need for extended timelines and increased budget, yet it deliberately did not discuss this matter with the petitioner. The petitioner has been diligently working on the project for the past 7 years and during this period, completed approximately 60% of the project, submitted performance guarantee amounting to approximately 26 Crore in their favour, made significant financial investments in the project, secured bank loans, and procured equipment in advance and accordingly, a vested right has accrued in their favour. The respondent No. 2, by issuing a directive, evidently aims to influence BPC's decision regarding its contractual obligations with NKFTCL, which is legally untenable. It is a well-established legal principle that the authorities, in the performance of their statutory or public duties, cannot allow themselves to be dictated by higher authorities, thereby compromising their independent judgment and discretion. 

28. Mr. Karim further submits that respondent No. 2, by dint of the impugned notices, intended to rescind its decision by instructing the respondent No.3 to terminate its contract with the respondent No.4. However, according to the principle of locus poenitentiae (i.e., an opportunity to withdraw from a contract or obligation before it is completed or to decide not to commit an intended crime), such action would be contingent upon the completion and decisiveness of the work performed under the initial contract. Despite the respondents' ongoing silence, the petitioner has consistently complied with all directives issued by the respondent Nos. 3 and 4. Moreover, the petitioner has periodically extended bank guarantees, made significant financial investments in the project, secured bank loans, and procured equipment in advance, which is currently stored in ports and warehouses. Respondent No. 2, while issuing the impugned notice, referred to a letter dated 28-5-2024 issued by BPC, which is the basis upon which the impugned letter was issued by the respondent No. 2 the concerned Ministry. BPC's letter does not make any specific reference or allegations as to how the petitioner, or as a matter of fact, the respondent No.4, was in breach of the contract. BPC's letter refers to the same discussions relating to expansion of budget and timeline as has been requested by the petitioner over the last one and half years and therefore, the decision of respondent No. 2 asking BPC to cancel its contract with NKFTCL is arbitrary and malafide as it has been issued to include a particular 'third-party' contractor instead of the petitioner. 

29. Mr. Karim further submits that the petitioner has acquired a vested and substantial interest in the project, which cannot be arbitrarily divested by the respondents, particularly because of the protections enshrined under section 202, read with section 65, of the Contract Act, 1872. The respondent No.3, having received and taken the benefit of the equipment and machinery imported by the petitioner, as well as having utilized the designs and drawings provided by the petitioner, is legally bound to restore or reimburse the petitioner under the principles of the doctrine of unjust enrichment and consequently, the petitioner is a party aggrieved party, and the instant writ petition is maintainable in law. 

30. Mr. Karim further submits that section 9 of the বিদ্যুৎ ও জ্বালানীর দ্রুত সরবরাহ বৃদ্ধি (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০১০ though now repealed, explicitly rendered actions taken under its provisions final and immune from challenge. This makes the impugned directive dated 26-6-2024, non-justiciable in arbitration proceedings because it was issued by the Government under the purview of this very Act. Therefore, arbitration is not an efficacious remedy for seeking legal redress against this specific Directive. Since the respondent No.3 terminated its contract with the respondent No.4 because of this government directive, and section 9 of the repealed Act precludes any challenge to such actions in other forums, the petitioner has no recourse before any forum other than the writ jurisdiction to address their grievance against the respondent No.3's actions. This effectively positions the writ petition as the only available legal avenue for the petitioner. 

31. Mr. Karimfurther submits that in the absence of a written agreement containing an arbitration clause, the petitioner is precluded from initiating arbitration proceedings against the Government or BPC as per section 27 of the Arbitration Act, 2001. Consequently, the arbitration proceedings already initiated by the petitioner under section 7Ka (for temporary relief/status quo) and section 12 (for arbitrator appointment) of the Arbitration Act, 2001, cannot have any nexus or direct relevance to the specific grievance raised in the instant writ petition. Furthermore, any order passed under section 7Ka is merely a temporary relief effective only until an arbitral tribunal is formed, rendering the argument of arbitration as an "alternative remedy" out of context for the core issues of the writ petition. 

32. Mr. Karim further submits that as evident from the impugned directive [Annexure G to the writ petition] and Government notification dated 9-10-2017 [Annexure B to the writ petition], the contract for the Project in question is rooted in বিদ্যুৎ ও জ্বালানীর দ্রুত সরবরাহ বৃদ্ধি (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০১০ since sections 4 to 7 of the Act of 2010 expressly empowers Statutory Bodies such as BPC to nominate/propose contractor for circulation and transpiration of fuel oil before ECNEC (Executive Committee of the National Economic Council). In the instant case, the respondent No.1-3 in exercise o fits power rooted in বিদ্যুৎ ও জ্বালানীর দ্রুত সরবরাহ বৃদ্ধি (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০১০ entered into a contract with EPC (Engineering, Procurement and Construction) contractor, the respondent No.4, NKFTCL. 

33. Mr. Karim further submits that the arbitration against the respondent No.4 would be ineffective because the respondent No.4 is, in practice, merely a welfare association with no substantive role or investment in the project beyond acting as an intermediary between the respondent No.3 and the petitioner. Consequently, any arbitral award against the respondent No.4 would fail to provide any meaningful remedy to the petitioner. This leaves the petitioner without any adequate or efficacious alternative remedy to judicially challenge the legality and propriety of the impugned notices, thereby making the instant writ petition maintainable. 

34. In support of the submissions, the learned Advocate of the petitioner, referred to the cases of Acqua Foods Limited and another vs Controller of Imports and Exports and others, reported in 49 DLR 498; Managing Director, Dhaka WASA Superior Builders and Engineers Ltd, reported in 51 DLR (AD) 56; IT, Dacca vs Mr. AW Mallik and others, reported in 20 DLR (SC) 229; Dr. Syed Matiur Rob being dead his heirs Shamsun Nahar & Others vs Bangladesh and others, reported in 9 BLD (AD) 52; Ministry of Industries, Nationalized Industries Division vs Saleh Ahmed & Another and Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation vs Saleh Ahmed and others, reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 91; Amir Hossain Sowdagar vs Md. Harunur Rashid and others, reported in 65 DLR (AD) 130; Pir Mohammad Farid Jan & others vs Colonisation Officer, Sukkur Barrage, Hyderabad and others, reported in 17 DLR SC 181; ABB India Limited vs Power Grid Company of Bangladesh Ltd and others, reported in 73 DLR 362; Privatization Board vs AK Fazlul Hug and another, reported in 55 DLR (AD) 11. 

35. Conversely, Mr. Ashraful Hadi, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No.3 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition, submits that the instant writ petition is not maintainable since that the impugned notice dated 26-6-2024 issued by the respondent No.2 is an inter-ministerial or inter department communication not addressed to the petitioner and the petitioner was not a party to it and, hence, the petitioner being a sub-sub-contractor does not have any locus standi, The impugned notice is a memo of approval purely related to the commercial contracts, and, as such, no writ lies against any alleged violation of such commercial contracts. The appropriate remedy lies in a civil jurisdiction, but not in a writ jurisdiction. The petitioner has admittedly filed several miscellaneous arbitration cases for the appointment of an arbitrator under section 12 of the Arbitration Act, 2001, and for ad-interim status quo under section 7Ka of the Arbitration Act, 2001. 

36. Mr. Ha di further submits that the contract and the revised contract in question were executed between the respondent No.3 and the Bangladesh Navy. The petitioner is neither a party to nor has any enforceable rights under the said contract or the revised Contract. The petitioner is claiming itself as a sub-sub-contractor under the said contract and revised contract, and, as such, the instant writ petition filed by a third-party stranger to such contracts is not maintainable as there is no privity of contract. 

37. Mr. Hadi further submits that the petitioner has alternative and efficacious remedy to address any of its grievance by way of filing civil proceedings or pursuing arbitration proceedings, which forums have already been availed and being continued by the petitioner by way of filing Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.407 of 2024 under section 12 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 for appointment of arbitrator impleading the respondent No.3 as the pro-forma opposite parties, and also by filing Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.33 of 2024 under section 7Ka of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and Civil Revision No.1839 of 2024. Thus, if the petitioner has any claim under its contract with the respondent No.4, it may raise such a claim before a duly constituted arbitral tribunal, and hence, the petitioner is not entitled to any relief under the instant writ petition and for the further reason that the matter involves disputed questions of fact and needs examination of evidence to adjudicate properly. 

38. Mr. Hadi further submits that the petitioner did not come before this court with clean hands since it has already entered into a partnership agreement dated 12-2-2023 with BCCL handing-over the entire responsibility of completion of the Project work on the ground of its incapacity as a sub-contractor to complete the Project work, and hence, the petitioner is in no way aggrieved by the impugned notice dated 26-6-2024 issued by the respondent No.2. Furthermore, its claim is liable to be barred under the doctrine of approbate and reprobate since it could not plead before this Hon'ble Court that it is a competent contractor, while on the other hand, enters into a private parties surrendering the contract being incapable to complete the project work. 

39. Mr. Hadi further submits that the impugned notice dated 26-6-2024 issued by the respondent No.2 is not dictated to the respondent No.3; rather, it approves the proposals of the respondent No.3 vide its letter dated 28-5-2024 seeking advice. Furthermore, the said letter properly set out the reasons that the respondent No.4 is reliant on a sub-contractor who is not competent to complete the Project work, and the revised proposal is exorbitantly high as suggested by PMC's report and consultation. Hence, there was a breach of the contract on the part of the respondent No.4, and there is no illegalityor mala fide intention on the part of the respondent No.3, rather the said decision was taken with a bona fide intention to save government money and to complete a highly critical Project work without causing any further delay. 

40. Mr. Hadi further submits that the instant writ petition is not maintainable under Article 102 of the Constitution because it constitutes a "cunning device tocircumvent orshort-cut" existing alternative legal proceedings. These include ongoing matters before the District Judge, Dhaka, the High Court Division, and the Arbitration Tribunal. It is further contended that the writ petition is an abuse of the court's process, designed to unduly influence those ongoing proceedings. Therefore, the instant writ petition has been filed in bad faith, making the rule issued in it not maintainable and liable to be discharged. 

41. In support of the submissions, the learned Advocate of the respondent No.3, referred to the cases of Nazrul Islam (Md) and another vs Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 58 DLR 431; Md. Mobarak Hossain vs Government of the Bangladesh and others, reported in 19 BLT (HCD) 54; NG Projects vs Vinod Kumar Jain and others, reported in AIR 2022 SC 1531; KS Rashid and Son vs The Income Tax Investigation Commission and others, reported in AIR 1954 SC 207; KPM Builders Private Limited vs National Highways Authority of India and another, reported in 15 SCC 394; Raj Kumar Bahal vs Food Corporation of India and others, reported in AIR 1990 Raj 64; Government of Bangladesh vs Kazi Mofizul Haque, reported in 20 ADC 879; Superintendent Engineer, RHD Sylhet & Others vs Md. Eunus and Brother (Pvt) Ltd. [Along with Civil Appeal Nos. 245-250 of 20051, reported in 16 BLC (AD) 73; Bangladesh Power Development Board and others vs Md. Asaduzzaman Sikder, reported in 9 BLC (AD) 1. 

42. Mr. Syed Ejaz Kabir, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent No.1 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition, submits that the writ petition is not maintainable because the petitioner, a sub-sub-contractor, lacks locus standi. This is due to the impugned memo being an internal, inter-departmental communication, not addressed to or involving the petitioner. Crucially, there's no privity of contract between the petitioner and the main contract parties (Respondent No. 3 and the Bangladesh Navy), meaning the petitioner has no enforceable rights under those agreements. Furthermore, the memo concerns commercial contracts, for which civil jurisdiction or arbitration are the appropriate remedies, not a writ petition. The petitioner is already pursuing alternative and efficacious remedies through multiple arbitration cases and a civil revision, indicating the dispute involves questions of fact better resolved in those forums. The impugned memo from Respondent No. 2 is defended as legitimate, being an approval of Respondent No.3's proposals, not a dictation. The decision was based on valid reasons that the Respondent No.4's reliance on an incompetent sub-contractor (the petitioner) and an exorbitantly high revised proposal. This action was taken with bona fide intention to save government funds and ensure the timely completion of a critical project, suggesting a breach of contract by Respondent No. 4 and no wrongdoing by Respondent No. 3, and, as such, the rules issued in the instant writ petition are liable to be discharged. In support of his submission, he cited the cases of Superintendent Engineer, RHD Sylhet & Others vs Md. Eunus and Brother (Pvt) Ltd. (Along with Civil Appeal Nos.245-250 of 2005), reported in 16 BLC (AD) 73; Bangladesh Power Development Board and others vs Md. Asaduzzaman Sikder, reported in 9 BLC (AD) 1.  
43. Heard the learned Advocates for the respective parties and perused the materials on record thoroughly. 

44. It appears from Annexure 2 to the affidavit-in-opposition that the respondent No.3 filed a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.2680 of 2024 before the Hon'ble Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, challenging the aforesaid interim order of stay dated 01-7-2024. Upon hearing both parties, the Full Bench of the Hon'ble Appellate Division, by its order dated 3-9-2024, was pleased to pass an order staying the operation of the ad-interim order of stay passed by the High Court Division till the disposal of the Rule. 

45. During the hearing, the respondent Nos.1 and 3 raised the question of the maintainability of the instant writ petition, and therefore, at first, this court wants to see whether the instant writ petition is maintainable in its present form and the learned Senior Counsel of the petitioner also conceded the same and after that, this court will enter into the merits of the writ petition for disposal. 

46. It appears that the petitioner is a joint venture (JV) entity named CMECC-BEL (JV), formed on 7-11-2017, by China Machinery Engineering & Construction Corporation (CMECC) and BARAKA Engineers Ltd. (BEL). Subsequent addenda on 10-11-2019 and 25-11-2021 amended the JV agreement, with BEL becoming the leading partner as per the second addendum. 

47. It further appears that the respondent No. 1 (the Government) decided, via a resolution dated 27-9-2017, to appoint Nou Kollan Foundation Trading Company Limited (NKFTCL) (respondent No. 4) as the Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) contractor for the Jet A-1 Pipeline Project (from Pitalganj to Kurimitola Aviation Depot, including pumping facilities). This appointment was made through the Direct Procurement Method (DPM) under the বিদ্যুৎ ও জ্বালানীর দ্রুত সরবরাহ বৃদ্ধি (বিশেষ বিধান) আইন, ২০১০. The respondent No.2-concerned Ministry, communicated this decision to the respondent No.3 on 9-10-2017. Following the government's decision, the respondent No.3 issued a Notification of Award to the respondent No. 4, and the project proceeded. Following the Notification of Award from the respondent No.3, NKFTCL (respondent No.4) engaged China Machinery Engineering and Construction Corporation (CMECC) for the Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) works of the Project. CMECC, in turn, formed a joint venture (JV) agreement with BARAKA Engineers Ltd. (BEL) on 7-11-2017, operating as CMECC-BELJV (the petitioner)for the completion of the Project and therefore, the petitioner became the sub-contractor of the respondent No.4. Thereafter, on 12-10-2017, the respondent No.4 communicated its letter of acceptance of the Notification of Award to the petitioner, who, in response, accepted it on the same day. Subsequently, on 9-11-2017, respondent No. 4 and the petitioner entered into a joint contract agreement for the Project. Initially, the Project was set for completion by 9-11-2018, with acostof BDT 1,833,381,644.77. A revised deed of agreement was executed between respondent No. 4 and the petitioner on 11-5-2022, rescheduling the Project completion within on 31-12-2022, and revising the budget to Taka 2,674,709,221.50. Following the revised agreement, the petitioner furnished two performance securities in the form of bank guarantees to respondent No.3, initially for Taka 183,338,165 (dated 11-4-2019) and subsequently for Taka 84,132,758 (dated 26-4-2022), both issued by Modhumoti Bank Limited, Gulshan Branch. These bank guarantees have been extended multiple times, most recently until 31-12-2024, at the request of NKFTCL. 

48. It further appears that the petitioner failed to complete the said work with in the stipulated time, and accordingly, respondent No.2 issue dadirective on 26-6-2024 (impugned Annexure-G to the writ petition), to cancel the contract with the respondent No.4. The petitioner subsequently learned that on 30-6-2024, the respondent No. 3 (BPC) terminated its contract agreement (dated 8-11-2017, and revised on 27-4-2022) with the respondent No.4 (NKFTCL) (impugned Annexure-L to the writ petition). Following this, on 3-7-2024, the respondent No.4, in turn, issued a termination notice to the petitioner, ending its contract agreements (dated 9-11-2017 and revised on 11- 5-2022) with the petitioner. This chain of events, where the respondent No.3's termination of its contract with the respondent No.4 (based on the 26-6-2024 directive) directly led to the respondent No.4 cancelling its contract with the petitioner, has caused the petitioner to be directly aggrieved, and this action is now the subject of the instant writ petition. 

49. It further appears that the petitioner has initiated the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.33 of 2024 on 22-1-2024 against the present respondent No.3, respondent No.4, respondent No.5, and respondent No.6 under section 7Ka of the Arbitration Act 2001 before the District Judge, Dhaka, who by its order dated 23-4-2024 in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.33 of 2024 admitted the above application and also issued show cause notice for 15 days, against which, the petitioner preferred a Civil Revision No.1839 of 2024 before the Hon'ble High Court Division, where in the Rule was issued and also passed an order of ad-interim injunction by restraining to encashment of the Bank Guarantee (Annexures-3, 4, 5 and 6 to the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No.3). 

50. It further transpires from Annexure-7 of the affidavit-in-opposition that the petitioner also issued a Notice of Arbitration dated 27-6-2024 to respondent No.4 and respondent No.6. Thereafter, the petitioner, on 30-6-2024, filed the instant Writ Petition No.8220 of 2024 in the High Court Division, challenging the impugned memos. Subsequently, the petitioner has filed another application under section 12 of the Arbitration Act 2001 for the appointment of an arbitrator (in which the respondent No.3 is a pro form arespondent), which is numbered as Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.407 of 2024 before the learned Court of District Judge, Dhaka. 

51. From the above facts, it transpires that there was no privity of contract between the petitioner and the respondent No.3. The contract and the revised contract in question were executed between the respondent No.3 and Bangladesh Navy, through the respondent No.4. Therefore, the petitioner, as a sub-sub-contractor, lacks locus standi and privity of contract. A contract creates rights and obligations only as between the parties to such a contract. As a corollary, a third party neither acquires a right nor any liabilities under such a contract. This is what the proclaimed doctrine of "privity of contract" enunciates and establishes as the overarching rule underlying any contractual relation. 

52. The impugned notice dated 26-6-2024, is an internal and inter-depart mental communication, not addressed to the petitioner, and the petitioner was not a party to the main contracts between respondent No. 3 and the Bangladesh Navy (Annexure-9 to the affidavit in-in-opposition of the respondent No.3). As such, the petitioner, being a third party to these core agreements, has no enforceable rights. 

53. The notices concern commercial contracts, for which a writ petition is generally not the appropriate remedy; civil jurisdiction or arbitration would be the proper remedy. The petitioner already has initiated alternative and efficacious remedies and is actively pursuing them through multiple arbitration cases (including Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.407 of 2024 for arbitrator appointment and Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.33 of 2024 for ad-interim status quo) and a Civil Revision No. 1839 of 2024. This indicates the matter involves disputed questions of fact best resolved in those forums. 

54. Given the presented facts, circumstances, and legal decisions from all parties, this court has come to the conclusion that the instant writ petition is not maintainable. As a result, we feel not necessary to delve into the merits of the case. Consequently, the Rule Nisi is liable to be discharged as not being maintainable. 

55. As a result, the Rule is discharged as not being maintainable. However, there is no order as to cost. 

Communicate the judgment and order at once. 

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1281 of 2018
lawyer:
Sk. Md Morshed, Additional Attorney-General instructed by Mahmuda Begum, Advocate-on-Record — For the Petitioners. 
Zainul Abedin, Advocate-on-Record —For Respondent No.1.

parties:
Government of Bangladesh and others ------- Petitioners
vs
Aruna Rani Sarker and another ------- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 27th day of March, 2017 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.1985 of 2014)
full_judgment:
Jahangir Hossain, J: Delay of 289 days under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908 in filing the instant civil petition for leave to appeal is hereby condoned. 

2. This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated the 27th day of March, 2017 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.1985 of 2014 making the Rule Nisi absolute. 

3. The facts, relevant for disposal of this petition, in brief, are that respondent No.01 as writ-petitioner filed Writ Petition No.1985 of 2014 stating, infer-alia, that she joined as Assistant Teacher of Shuvesha Shishu Registered Non-Government Primary School, Bagerhat Sadar, Bagerhat on 7-8-1999. She received the Monthly Payment Order [MPO] vide index No. 210743 with effect from the month of August, 2000 to September, 2013 and she has been serving in the said institution with utmost honesty and sincerity. 

4. The Managing Committee appraised her promotion as Headmistress in the said school from the post of Assistant Teacher and she joined on 12-7-2012 in the new post. After joining the new post, she applied for fixation of her monthly salary as Headmistress through the Chairman of the Managing Committee of the said school on 4-5-2013. It is further contended that the writ-petitioner from time to time personally persuaded the concerned officer for the payment of her salary as per scale prescribed by the government but got no result. She received her monthly salary upto the month of September, 2013. Subsequently, she did not receive any salary, not only as Headmistress but also as an Assistant Teacher. The writ-petitioner used to receive a sum of Taka 5,194 as her monthly salary as Assistant Teacher and after getting promotion, she was entitled to get the scale being 5,500 — 345 x 4915 EB 380 x 11 and also entitled to get the gross salary amounting to 12,095. The Chairman of the Managing Committee by a DO letter dated 4-5-2013 requested the Secretary, Primary and Mass Education for payment of the monthly payment order to the writ-petitioner but the request resulted in vain. The writ-petitioner again and again tried her best to get her salary but failed. Having no other alternative remedies, the writ-petitioner moved the High Court Division and obtained the Rule Nisi in the form of mandamus. 

5. Writ-respondent No.5, Nasira Khatun, after issuance of the Rule Nisi, filed an application for addition of a party to contest the Rule Nisi. Accordingly, the application was allowed. Writ-respondent No.5 contested the Rule Nisi by filing affidavit-in-opposition, contending, inter-alia, that she joined as Assistant Teacher of Shuvesha Shishu Registered Non-Government Primary School on 15-1-1989 and after completing all formalities, she received the monthly payment order and she has been serving in the said institution since the time of her joining. On 8-4-2008, the president of the Managing Committee of the Shuvesha Shishu Registered Primary School appointed the applicant, i.e. writ-respondent No.5 as Headmistress-in-charge of the said school. She filed an application against the writ-petitioner to the District Education Officer who made a two members inquiry committee vide office letter dated 8-122010 under Memo No. জেপ্রাশিঅ/বাগের/১৪৭১/৪. On completion of the inquiry, the inquiry committee submitted the inquiry report dated 26-1-2011 and opined that the appointment of said Aruna Rani Sarkar, as Headmistress, was not held properly and accordingly, the said report was forwarded to the District Education Officer, Bagerhat and also to the Director General of Primary and Mass Education Department, Dhaka vide Memo No. জেপ্রাশিঅ/বাগের/৬৩ dated 30-1-2011. Though the writ-petitioner, Aruna Rani Sarkar, applied for fixation of her monthly salary as Headmistress to the authority concerned, but the Deputy Director, Khulna Division, rejected her application vide letter dated 21-4-2013 under Memo No. বাপ্রাশি/৩৮.২৪৯.০০১.০৪.০০.০৩৪.২০১২/৭৬৪ and the same was intimated to the Upazila Education Officer, Sadar, Bagerhat. The present applicant [writ-respondent Noll was perfor-ming her function sincerely as Headmistress-in-charge, but the writ-petitioner, Aruna Rani Sarkar, suppressing all facts filed the writ petition without making the applicant, a party with a view to keeping her out of scene so that the applicant could not contest the writ petition. As the applicant had been working in the said school as Headmistress-in-charge, it was necessary to make her party for proper adjudication and disposal of the writ petition, but the writ-petitioner did not make her a party to the writ petition with mala-fide intention to restrain her from contesting the writ petition. Ultimately she was made party to the writ petition as respondent No.5 on her application. 

6. However, the High Court Division after hearing the parties and on perusal of the materials on record, made the Rule Nisi absolute by its judgment and order dated 27-3-2017. 

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and order dated 27-3-2017, respondent No. 1[Government] to the writ petition as leave petitioner filed the instant civil petition for leave to appeal before this Division to seek redress.  

8. Mr SK. Md Morshed, learned Additional Attorney-General, appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submits that the High Court Division misread and misinterpreted the materials on record and relevant laws of the case in question and non-judicially passed the impugned judgment and order. He further submits that the High Court Division did not properly peruse the evidence on record and misdirected themselves from the facts and circumstances of the case. It is further submitted that the High Court Division failed to take into consideration the facts and circumstances of the case and material points of the case on record and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is not at all sustainable in law. 

9. Per contra, Mr Zainul Abedin, Advocate-on-Record, appearing on behalf of present respondent No. 01, contends that the High Court Division having examined all the papers and documents on record and hearing the parties, rightly passed the impugned judgment and order making the Rule Nisi absolute. Since there is no illegality in passing the judgment and order of the High Court Division, no question arises for interference by this Division. 

10. Heard the contentions of the learned Advocates and perused the materials on record along with impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division. 

11. It appears that the writ-petitioner joined as an Assistant Teacher in Shuvesha Shishu Registered Non-Government Primary School, Bagerhat Sadar, Bagerhat on 7-8-1999. She got promotion as Headmistress. She applied for fixation of her salary, i.e. Monthly Payment Order for her new post as Head-mistress but present petitioner No.2 herein stopped her salary, i.e. Monthly Payment Order. She approached the concerned authority to resolve the issue but the step went in vain. 

12. On the contrary, the claim of the government, i.e. the present petitioners is that granting MPO is the policy decision of the government. The factual aspects brought out by the writ-petitioner cannot be considered in the nature of mandamus. It is obvious that sanction of Monthly Payment Order depends on the decision of the Government. There is no enforceable right of any person in the law to get entitlement of MPO or its enhancement because it has financial involvement in meeting up the same. 

13. In the case of Government of Bangladesh and others vs Md Nazrul Islam and others, reported in 27 BLT (AD) 167 : 26 BLC (AD) 334, this Division also observed that—
"In the case in hand the petitioners did not allege that the writ respondents have violated any legal right of them. The granting of MPO is the policy decision of the Government. Therefore, the petitioners could not claim the same as of right. This Division is of the view that teachers and staffs of the Non-Government School and College could not claim the MPO as a matter of right and, as such, direction could not be given unless infringement of legal right or violation of law." 

14. Moreover, having gone through the provision of section 18(6) of the Jonabal Kathamo, 2010 [as amended in 2013] it appears that there is a restriction imposed by law to withdraw the salary, i.e. the Monthly Payment Order if there are disputes in the internal management of the institution. It has been enshrined in section 18(6) of the Jonabal Kathamo, 2010 that— "(৬) প্রতিষ্ঠানের শিক্ষক/কর্মচারী ব্যবস্থাপনা কমিটির মধ্যকার অভ্যন্তরীণ বিরোধের কারণে বা তাদের মধ্যে সৃষ্ঠ মামলার বা অন্য কোন কারণে বেতন-ভাতাদির সরকারী অংশ উত্তোলন সম্ভব না হলে পরবর্তীতে বকেয়া হিসাবে তা উত্তোলন করা যাবে না। সংশ্লিষ্ট প্রতিষ্ঠান এর আর্থিক দায়-দায়িত্ব বহন করবে।" In the instant case, we have already found that appointment of the writ-petitioner was not made in accordance with rules. Nonetheless, an inquiry was initiated against the writ-petitioner for practicing fraud upon suppressing all facts while filing the writ petition without making the Headmistress-in-charge of the institution, a party with a view to keeping her out of scene so that the Headmistress-in-charge could not contest the writ petition. So, there has been no illegality in stopping the MPO of the writ-petitioner. It further reveals that the writ-petitioner did not mention in the writ petition regarding the inquiry pending against her and if the writ-petitioner disclosed the facts of the inquiry pending against her, the result of the Rule Nisi might have been otherwise. However, it is a disputed question of fact against which the writ-petition in the form of mandamus is not maintainable. The writ-petitioner did not also come with clean hands before the Court of law. 

15. Having considered all the aspects and discussions made above, we are constrained to hold that the writ-petition filed by the writ-petitioner was not maintainable. Therefore, we find merit in the present leave petition. However, it is better to dispose of the same without granting leave as the writ petition was not maintainable. 

Accordingly, this petition is disposed of. The judgment and order dated 27-3-2017 of the High Court Division is, hereby, set-aside. 

End.
