full_judgment:
Application for vacating order for arrest: 1st defendant vessel MV DK 03 (previous name MV Bianco Zealand) (IMO No. 9082908, Flag: Panama), on an application of the plaintiff, was arrested in Bangladesh on 4-8-2025. The added defendant No. 2B PT KYK Lines of JI, based in Indonesia, has filed an application for vacating the order for arrest. The application is contested by the plaintiff by filing written objection. During the course of hearing of the application, both parties filed bundles of documents by way of "List of Documents" (LoD) in support of their respective cases. The plaint has been amended three times. 'Plaint' referred to hereinafter means 'plaint' as it stands after the last amendment. 

Plaintiff's Case: 
2. Plaintiff is SEA PRIORITY SA, a company incorporated under the laws of Panama. The plaintiff claims that they are the registered owner of the 1st defendant vessel which was sold in a judicial proceedings in Sudan and defendant No. 2B, who claims to be the subsequent purchaser and owner of the vessel (probably 4th-hand purchaser), did not acquire any valid title in the vessel on the grounds, inter alia, that the judicial sale in Sudan was tainted with fraud, the proceedings followed in Sudan were opposed to the principle of natural justice and defendant No. 2B has failed to establish the chain of title. 

Plaintiff's prayer in the suit: 
3. The plaintiff has made two prayers in the plaint. Those are: — 
(a) to declare that the plaintiff is and has always been the lawful owner of the 1st defendant vessel; 
(b) to pass an order directing that possession of the vessel be handed over to the plaintiff, and to permit the plaintiff or its authorized local representatives to assume full management and operational control thereof. 

4. The case is still at the pre-trial stage. Defendant No. 2B has not yet filed written statement. 

Facts: 
5. Relevant facts are gathered from the plaint and documents filed by the parties. I have particularly relied upon the plaint and notarized statements of Mr. Osman Mohamed Elsharief Elnour who represented the claimant Al-Hamama Grain Mills Project (Al-Hamama) in Sudan Court proceedings as their lawyer. 

6. The plaintiff company became the registered owner of the vessel on 15-11-2024. They voyage chartered the vessel to VA Intertrading Aktiengesellschaft, Linz, Austria on 6-2-2016 for a voyage from Russia to Port Sudan to deliver 45,000 mts of bulk milling wheat. The freight was pre-paid. The bill of lading, which was issued on 3-3-2016 by the master of the vessel, incorporated the charterparty dated 6-2-2016. Al-Hamama was the endorsee of the bill of lading. 

7. On 11-4-2016, the plaintiff instructed the master of the vessel not to cross the Suez Channel due to a dispute with the charterers and the receivers. At the request of the charterers, the master had a meeting with the charterers and receivers on board the vessel. It appears that the charterers and receivers paid Suez Channel passage fees and crews' unpaid wages in cash without approval of the plaintiff. The master informed the plaintiff and others including Al-Hamama of the matter. Despite the plaintiff's specific instructions to the contrary, the vessel crossed the Suez Channel and arrived at Port Sudan. A delay of 45 days occurred in reaching the vessel in Sudan. 

8. Al-Hamama as claimant filed a case before the Port Sudan Civil Court against the owners of the vessel Bianco Zealand through its captain as defendant (present plaintiff) for USD 243,773 which includes attorney's fees of USD 50,000. It is stated in the said petition of claim that the claimant paid the Suez Canal transit fees, seamen's wages and Port Sudan port fees and that the 45-day delay in the vessel's arrival at the port and the delay in unloading the cargo due to unavailability of equipments on board the vessel caused financial loss to the claimant. The vessel was arrested at Port Sudan on 25-5-2016.
 
9. It is averred in the plaint that during the proceedings in Sudan from 2016 to 2018, the master continued to represent the owners of the vessel in the Court. The present plaintiff initially appointed local lawyers to defend itself in the Sudanese Court proceedings. In late 2016, the plaintiff appointed Mr. Elie Medlej who took over the case on or about 12-1-2017. On 18-7-2017, the plaintiff notified the claimant (Al-Hamama) and their lawyer Mr. Elsharief and the Court that the master and his lawyer did not represent the owner Sea Priority SA (plaintiff). Despite the notice, the Sudanese Court continued to recognize the master as representative of the Owners (plaintiff). The plaintiff attempted to secure the release of the vessel by offering a P&I Club Eetter of Undertaking and a surety bond. The plaintiff's P&I club confirmed on or about 24-1-2017 that international banks would refuse payment related to Sudan. 

10. It is stated in the statements of Mr. Elsharief Elnour (lawyer for Al-Hamama) that on 5-4-2017, the lawyer acting for the master offered a settlement to Al-Hamama who agreed to waive its claim for compensation, and a "consent judgment" was accordingly awarded. The Owners, Sea Priority did not appeal against the consent judgment. In any event, a consent judgment cannot be appealed under the Sudanese law. 

11. Owners Sea Priority (present plaintiff) failed to satisfy the consent judgment and did not furnish guarantee or security in the sum stipulated under the consent judgment for the release of the vessel. The claimant Al-Hamama initiated enforcement proceedings. On 10-3-2017, the Sudanese Maritime Administration assessed the vessel's value based on its operation at USD 2,600,000 and scrap value at USD 1,467,072, with a 2% appraisal fee proposed. The Court ordered that the vessel to be sold at public auction. 

12. The first auction was held on 17-12-2017 at a base price for USD 2,600,000, but no bidders attended the auction. 

13. Second auction was held in January, 2018 at a reduced base price for USD 2,500,000. Again, no bidders attended. 

14. Third auction, with the base price reduced to USD 1,700,000, was held on 7-2-2018. Two bidders participated. The highest bidder failed to pay the requisite 20% deposit within 24 hours and the bid was cancelled. 

15. Fourth auction was held on 5-3-2018 at the same base price for USD 1,700,000. Ali Saif Mohammed Said Al-Ghafli was the successful bidder, the bid price being USD 1,710,000. He paid the deposit, and complied with all conditions of sale. The sale proceeds were deposited in the Court for distribution among the creditors. 

16. On 29-3-2018, the Court of Sudan issued the vessel's 'Sale Certificate' in the buyer's name stating, "It is free from all debts and prohibitions that impede its registration in the buyer's name". On 2-4-2018, a new certificate of registry in respect of the Vessel was issued to the buyer. 

17. On 19-7-2018, a report was issued by a Court staff to the Judge recording that the total sale proceeds were USD 1,710,000, total payments (including Court fees and most crew wages) amounted to USD 421,368.43, and the balance held by the Court was USD 1,288,632.43 with outstanding wages for two crews totalling USD 347,136. 

Common law principles are applicable laws: 
18. During the course of argument, learned Counsels of both sides referred to numerous case laws. They accept that the principles of common law are the applicable laws in the case. 

Section 13 of CPC: 
19. Section 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC) of Bangladesh incorporates the principle of private international law that the Court will enforce a foreign judgment if it has been passed by a competent Court. The rules laid down in section 13 are rules of substantive law and not of mere procedure. Section 13 runs as follows: -- 
"13. When foreign judgment not conclusive —A foreign judgment shall be conclusive as to any matter thereby directly adjudicated upon between the same parties or between parties under whom they or any of them claim litigating under the same title except-
(a) where it has not been pronounced by a Court of competent jurisdiction; 
(b) where it has not been given on the merits of the case; 
(c) where it appears on the face of the proceedings to be founded on an incorrect view of international law or a refusal to recognise the law of Bangladesh in cases in which such law is applicable; 
(d) where the proceedings in which the judgment was obtained are opposed to natural justice; 
(e) where it has been obtained by fraud, 
(f) where it sustains a claim founded on a breach of any law in force in Bangladesh". 

20. Mr. Rahman, on behalf of the plaintiff, relies upon clauses (d) and (e) to section 13 in support of his case. 

21. Mr. Kadir, learned Counsel appearing for the defendant No. 2B, submits that the proposition of law at the common law is well established and has become a trite law that the title of a vessel given by a judicial sale is a valid title and must not be disturbed. Mr. Kadir points out that the defendant No. 2B is the 4th-hand purchaser of the vessel, the chain of title being rooted in the judicial sale in Sudan. 

The Tremont: 
22. At common law, the legal effect of judicial sale of a vessel has long been recognised. Referring to the judicial sale and its consequences, Dr. Lushington said in The Tremont (1841) 1 W Rob 163:—
"The jurisdiction of the Court in these matters is confirmed by the municipal law of this country and by the general principles of the maritime law; and the title conferred by the Court in the exercise of this authority is a valid title against the whole world, and is recognised by the Courts of this country and by the Courts of all other countries". 

Castrique vs Imrie: 
23. In Castrique vs Imrie, (1869) LR 4 HL 414 at page 429, Lord Blackburn laid down two conditions for determination as to when judicial sale of a vessel should be recognised. Lord Blackburn said: — 
"We think the inquiry is, first, whether the subject matter was so situated as to be within the lawful control of the state under the authority of which the Court sits; and, secondly, whether the sovereign authority of that state has conferred on the Court jurisdiction to decide as to the disposition of the thing, and the Court has acted within its jurisdiction. If these conditions are fulfilled, the adjudication is conclusive against all the world". 

The Acrux (No. 2): 
24. In The Acrux (No. 2) [19621 1 Lloyd's Rep. 405, the vessel Acrux was sold by the Admiralty Marshal of England. Subsequently, the mortgagees initiated a motion in the Admiralty Court of England for judgment in default of appearance against the proceeds of sale, with priorities reserved. Proceeds of sale were lesser than the sum claimed by mortgagees. The purchaser of the vessel Acrux was unable to secure permanent registration of the vessel in the desired country because he was unable to obtain certificate of deletion from Italian Register for the reason that the order for sale of Admiralty Court of England was not recognized in Italy. According to the Italian law, mortgagees could proceed against the ship in any country. Mr. Justice Hewson referred to The Tremont and Castrique vs Imrie and said: — 
"As I see it, the title to the Acrux was given to an innocent- purchaser, and the money he paid is in this Court to satisfy all legitimate claims regardless of the nationality of the plaintiffs according to their priorities. 
The title given by such process is a valid title and must not be disturbed by those who have knowledge or who may receive knowledge of the proceedings in this Court. 
So far as all claimants against this ship before her arrest are concerned, their claims are now against the fund in this Court and not against the ship properly sold to an innocent purchaser free of incumbrances. 
Were such a clean title as given by this Court to be challenged or disturbed, the innocent purchaser would be gravely prejudiced. Not only that, but as a general proposition the maritime interests of the world would suffer. Were it to become established, contrary to general maritime law, that a proper sale of a ship by a competent Court did not give a clean title, those whose business it is to make advances of money in their various ways to enable ships to pursue their lawful occasions would be prejudiced in all cases where it became necessary to sell the ship under proper process of any competent Court. 
It would be intolerable, inequitable and an affront to the Court if any party who invoked the process of this Court and received its aid and, by implication, assented to the sale to an innocent purchaser, should thereafter proceed or was able to proceed elsewhere against the ship under her new and innocent ownership. This Court recognizes proper sales by competent Courts of Admiralty, or Prize, abroad-it is part of the comity of nations as well as a contribution to the general well-being of international maritime trade". 

The "Cerro Colorado"; principle of comity: 
25. In The "Cerro Colorado" [1993] 1 Lloyd's Rep. 58, Mr. Justice Sheen observed that the general principles of maritime law to which Dr Lushington referred in The Tremont are now embodied in the International Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules Relating to the Arrest of Seagoing Ships, 1952. Mr. Justice Sheen in his judgment quoted the passage from The Acrux and said: — "I adopt what was said by Mr. Justice Hewson. I can only express the hope that the Spanish Court will, as a matter of comity, recognise the decrees made by this Court, which endeavours to give effect to the International Arrest Convention". 

26. I note that Sudan is not a party to the 1952 Arrest Convention. However, Sudan is a party to the 1999 Convention on Arrest of Ships. Bangladesh is not a party to any of the conventions. Therefore, the principle of comity of nations shall apply to the instant case. 

The "Phoenix"; application of local law: 
27. In BCEN-Eurobank now known as VTB Bank (France) SA vs Vostokrybprom Co Ltd and ors. (The "Phoenix"), 1201411 Lloyd's Rep. 449, it was argued, among other things, that the judicial sale of the vessel 'Phoenix' in North Korea should not be recognised because the sale was not in accordance with settled procedures for forced sale in the UK or St Vincent and the Grenadines; the sale was in breach of the principles of natural justice because the bank had no notice of the sale; and the order for sale was based on dishonesty. It was prayed that the Court could not grant a declaration that Apex was the owner of the vessel free from all encumbrances. 

28. The Court of first instance of St Vincent and the Grenadines rejected the arguments and granted the declaration sought by Apex. The Court of first instance observed that it is a general rule that a judgment in rem of a foreign Court of competent jurisdiction in respect of a maritime lien was regarded as binding against all the world provided that the foreign Court had jurisdiction to hear the claim; the judgment was final and conclusive by the laws of the state in which it was given; and the judgment was not based on fraud or contrary to the rules of natural justice. The Court of first instance further observed that on the evidence, the bank had failed to establish that there had been a breach of the rules of natural justice so far as the judgment of the North Korea Court was concerned, nor had the bank adduced any evidence that the judicial sale had not been conducted in accordance with the procedure of the laws of North Korea, or that the bank was prevented from participating in the process of making a claim on the proceeds of the sale after it became aware of the sale. Courts would not invalidate a judicial sale that had been conducted in accordance with the procedure of the laws of that state. 

29. On appeal, the Court of Appeal of St Vincent and the Grenadines of Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court referred to the cases of The Tremont, Castrique vs Imrie, The Acrux (No. 2) and The Cerro Colorado and affirmed the judgment of the Court of first instance. The Court of Appeal observed at para 40:—
"In conclusion, a foreign judicial sale is to be recognised and given effect qua assignment/transfer of title unless it is invalid under the law of the country where the sale took place. There was no plea or evidence that such was the case in respect of either of the judicial sales at issue at the trial. The prime consideration is whether the transaction was valid under local law". 

Application of principle of comity in Bangladesh and India: 
30. The principle of comity of nations in respect of the general principles of maritime law has been recognised and applied by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in Rich Step Shipping Ltd. vs MV Ocean Dawning, 2015 (23) BLT (AD) 302 where the Appellate Division rejected the argument that no notice of sale of the vessels was served upon the plaintiffs. It was held that whether notice of sale was served or not is a matter not to be decided by the Court because the judicial sale took place in North Korea. 

31. After the decision of the Appellate Division, the 3rd defendant (subsequent purchaser of the vessel) filed an application for rejection of the plaint. The Admiralty Court of Bangladesh observed that the plaintiff had prayed for declaration of title of the 1st defendant vessel which was sold in North Korea in a judicial process and the auction purchaser in North Korea obtained the title of the vessel who sold it to the 3rd defendant. Accordingly, there was no cause of action to file the suit for declaration of title. The plaint was rejected. The decision is reported in 2016 (24) BLT (HCD) 140 (New Camp Shipping Ltd. vs MV Ocean Gataxi).
 
32. In Sparebanken Sogn Og Fjordance vs MV Bos Angler, 2013 (3) All MR 119, a Division Bench of the High Court of Bombay of India observed, —
"When the Court orders the sale of the vessel, it has the inherent power in the exercise of its admiralty jurisdiction to convey upon the purchaser a valid title to the res... This principle was established in the common law as one fundamental to public policy, since it would be manifestly contrary to the evolution of maritime law if a Court of competent jurisdiction which effected the sale of a ship were unable to convey a valid title to an innocent purchaser". 

Argument on behalf of plaintiff: 
33. Mr. Rahman, appearing for the plaintiff, neither disputes the ratio laid down by Dr. Lushington in The Tremont nor the two-fold test laid down by Lord Blackburn in Castrique vs Imrie. Mr. Rahman accepts that the principles established at common law apply in full force in appropriate facts and circums-tances of a case. Mr. Rahman argues that the present case is an exception for the following reasons: — 
(a) plaintiff, who was admittedly the registered owner of the vessel prior to the judicial sale in Sudan, was denied by the Sudanese Court to represent it in the Court proceedings. The master fraudulently represented the vessel in spite of objection given by the plaintiff. Thus, there was violation of the principle of natural justice which attracts clause (d) to section 13 of the Civil Procedure Code (CPC) of Bangladesh; 
(b) judicial sale in Sudan was procured by fraud which satisfies clause (e) to section 13 of the CPC. Fraud vitiates everything; 
(c) defendant No. 2B is not a bonafide purchaser for value without notice and has failed to establish that their chain of title is rooted in and/or connected to the auction purchaser in Sudan which they are required to do as per the decision given in MV Ocean Dawning (2015) 23 BLT (AD) 302 by our Appellate Division; 
(d) Sudanese Court did not have jurisdiction to proceed with the case as the relevant bill of lading incorporated the arbitration clause contained in the voyage charterparty, and lastly; 
(e) the judicial sale in Sudan was done in violation of the prohibition order passed on 29-4-2016 by a Panamanian Court. 

Representation in Sudan Court, application of Sudanese laws: 
34. Mr. Elsharief Elnour, who was the lawyer for the claimant Al-Hamama in Sudan Court case, has confirmed that the Civil Procedure Act, 1983 and Maritime Carriage Act, 2010 of Sudan allow the master to appear before the Court as legal representative of the owners of the vessel. Throughout the proceedings in Sudan, the master represented the owners. Mr. Elnour further confirms that two lawyers claimed to act for the owners Sea Priority (present plaintiff) through a power of attorney issued by the owners, but the Court rejected the representation because the power-of-attorney was not certified by the Sudanese Embassy or Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The master's appearance was recognized as the valid representation on behalf of the owners. Mr. Rahman could not rebut the statements of Mr. Elnour by producing any evidence. In this regard, I make it clear that Mr. Elnour's statements relate to statements of facts concerning chronological events that occurred in the Sudan Court. 

35. The present plaintiff, in their plaint, admitted that they were aware of the Sudanese Court proceedings and initially engaged local lawyers who were replaced by Mr. Medlej in late 2016. The plaintiff's P&I Club refused on or about 24-1-2017 to issue letter of undertaking. According to the statements made in the plaint, "plaintiff maintained sufficient financial capacity and available cash balances to remit the demanded funds including the illicit expenses", but they expressly refused to do so on "ethical grounds to participate in this corrupt scheme or to remit funds for the purpose of bribing foreign officials. The transaction failed solely due to this ethical refusal" (para 16C). 

'Consent Judgment' in Sudan: 
36. 'Consent judgment' was obtained in Sudan in April, 2017. The plaintiff unsuccessfully appealed. The plaintiff requested the Sudanese Court to suspend the enforcement and sale proceedings. The request was rejected. The plaintiff again unsuccessfully appealed. Eventually, the vessel was sold to a private individual on or about 5-3-2018 at the fourth auction. 

'Court-assisted sale'/'staged auction': 
37. Earlier, the plaintiff's lawyer in Sudan Mr. Medlej pursued a strategy invoking a 'Court-assisted sale' or 'staged auction' whereby the vessel would be sold through Sudanese Court to a company 'Ashanti' nominated by the plaintiff. This process evolved into a corrupt scheme. The plaintiff did not accept the initiative on ethical grounds (para 16 of the plaint). 

Alleged violation of principle of natural justice: 
38. Mr. Rahman argues that the above-stated facts satisfy clauses (d) and (e) to section 13 of the CPC i.e., violation of principle of natural justice and fraud. I do not accept the argument for reason that the principle of comity of nations demands that the law of the country where the judicial sale takes place has to be recognised and given effect quo assignment/transfer of title (The "Phoenix"). The master of the vessel represented the plaintiff in Sudan in accordance with the law of Sudan. Plaintiff had notice of it and unsuccessfully attempted to represent itself in the Court. Everything was done as per the law of Sudan. The plaintiff successfully objected and postponed the initial public judicial auction scheduled for 19-12-2017 (para 14 of plaint). In Rich Step Shipping Ltd. vs MV Ocean Dawning, our Apex Court did not consider the question as to whether notice of sale was served upon the plaintiffs. Accordingly, I hold that there was no violation of the principle of natural justice in Sudanese Court proceedings. 

Alleged fraud, e-mail and WhatsApp messages: 
39. Now, I turn to the second limb of Mr. Rahman's argument regarding fraud. At para Nos. 16, 16A and 16B of the plaint, communi-cations between Mr. Medlej (plaintiff's lawyer in Sudan) and plaintiff's representative Mr. Stavros have been referred to in support of the alleged fraud or corrupt scheme. On going through the print out of various e-mails and WhatsApp messages contained in LoD No. 
9454 dated 10-11-2025 and LoD No. 10437 dated 3-12-2025 filed by the plaintiff, it appears that the communications have been mentioned in the plaint in a piecemeal fashion which do not reveal a complete picture. 

40. Section 126 of the Evidence Act, 1872 of Bangladesh safeguards the professional communications between the lawyer and his client from disclosure as 'privileged communication'. Section 126 further provides that if the client expressly consents to disclosure the protection is lifted. Since Mr. Rahman has produced the professional communications by way of LoD, I can certainly refer to and discuss those in my judgment. 

41. The communications disclosed by the plaintiff, in my view, do not reveal any fraud or corrupt scheme in the judicial sale in Sudan, rather those communications show that the plaintiff was all along in contact with their lawyer and was well aware of the up to date situation of the auction process. The following are examples:—
On 27-12-2017, John Papapetros, Partner of V & P Law Firm in Greece wrote to Mr. Stavros (plaintiff's representative), "we as your lawyers, strictly advise you and your companies against any illicit payment to the judge or to any third party in Sudan or elsewhere and against such kind of purchase in general". 
On 6-2-2018 at 10:36 (day before 3rd auction) Stavros wrote to Elie Medlej (plaintiff's lawyer in Sudan), "POA of Ashanti (the Buyer) will be apostiled by the Marshal Islands, the Sudanese embassy and the Greek Minister of Foreign Affairs". 
On 6-2-2018 at 18:35, Stavros again wrote to Elie Medlej, "Funds will be ready within the next two weeks all going well. Until then we either have to postpone the auction for a couple of weeks, preferably until March or negotiate a settlement in these 'auction' figures with the claimants". 
On 22-2-2018, Elie Medlej wrote to Stavros, "the committee accepted USD 1,705,000 for Ashanti. This has to be sanctioned by the Court on payment of the Deposit. There will be cost associated. So the Court will not sanction it unless the cost is guaranteed. As at this stage, it is USD 2.1 m in total. 
IT is very simple but unfortunately you ignore what I say and you think you can play with the Sudanese because you look down at them. I keep saying we are in Sudan and not in Denmark, so the systems are totally different, but please do not underestimate them". 
On 25-2-2018, Elie Medlej wrote to Stavros, "We met with the judge today who was extremely disappointed that Ashanti had not paid the Deposit yet. The judge, therefore, set a hearing for tomorrow morning in which he will fix a new date for the committee to convene and sell the ship again. 
We argued with the judge that Ashanti is ready to put up the Deposit but the judge advised that unless Ashanti pays the whole balance before the day the committee. will be convened, then he will not stop the re-auctioning of the Vessel". 
On 28-2-2018, Elie Medlej wrote to Stavros, "as it is a sale through the Court, then the Court requires it to be paid into the Court and not to be held by a private person". 

42. WhatsApp messages exchanged (dates could not be ascertained) between Elie Medlej and Stavros are as follows:— 
Stavros: How can the Court make a decision to sell the ship today?And how is it not possible for us to intervene and block this sale as we did last time? 
Elie: Stavros it is no longer a normal procedure as I have been telling you. We reached this mess so as to give you the solution you wanted... 
Stavros: Then if it is not a normal procedure then we can appeal it. Correct? 
Elie: There is a limit to the miracles we can do. Enjoy the beginning of the lent and let us communicate I the afternoon. 
Elie: Secure the money to a company in UAE before Thursday and I will secure the ship. I am a lawyer and not an exchange bureau. Your delay and your misleading us let us to this. 
Stavros: Can you find me a serious company like wilhemsen or Atlantic which is legit to send the money to? And who can guarantee that the funds will be used for the intended scope and in case the ship is not secured the funds will be returned? Elie: If we are to participate we need to have the Deposit by Thursday in Sudan / Dubai account. Then we need to fix the auction like last time, if possible. Stavros: The deal went to 2.1 million from 2 million last week in order to secure the deal. We did not secure the deal because you say you will try. 
Stavros: Under pressure here funds have left the account yet nothing from Sudan. 
Elie: Funds not received yet and anyway they will be with our guy and we will be careful before we pay inro the Court particularly as regards the deadline for the payment kf the balance and if you cannot meet with it. I will report to you in the evening. 
Elie: No news means bad news. 
Elie: Elie please send to Stavros an email or msg that remittance should be tomorrow this is the only chance. If no swift tomorrow it will be a problem. 
Elie: I am forwarding to you verbatim what I received from my colleague who is now in Sudan. 
Elie: I hope you are well as I have not heard from you. 

Reasonableness test: 
43. A reasonable man having working knowledge of judicial process, on going through the communications, is likely to think that the plaintiff and their lawyer attempted to manipulate the auction process and even at one stage, they succeeded, but eventually failed not on 'ethical grounds' as averred in the plaint but for other reasons. 

Arbitration clause: 
44. Clause 17 of the voyage charterparty dated 6-2-2016 containing arbitration clause, which was incorporated in the bill of lading, runs as follows: — 
"Any dispute arising out of the present contract shall be referred to arbitration in London/UK. The decision rendered according to English Law shall be final and binding upon both parties. The right of both parties to refer any disputes to arbitration ceases twelve months after date of completion of discharge or, in case of cancellation or non performances, twelve months after the cancelling date as per clause 6 or after the actual date of cancellation whichever is the later. Where the provision is not complied with, the claim shall be deemed to be waived and absolutely barred". 

45. The vessel was arrested in Sudan on 25-5-2016. 'Consent judgment' in Sudan was passed in April, 2017. On 6-7-2017, the plaintiff sent an e-mail to the representative of the claimant Al-Hamama stating, "Dear Sirs, Please note that despite our numerous reminders and efforts, you keep the vessel MN BIANCO ZEALAND under arrest refusing to accept the LOU issued by a major P&I and insurance company. This is in breach of your contractual obligations under the bills of lading contract and many well known decisions under English law. For all the above, kindly note that as per clause 17 of the CP dated 6-02-2016 which is fully incorporated under the bills of lading, today we have appointed Mr. Patrick O'Donovan as arbitrator in the case. All Owners' rights are reserved. Best Regards, Sea Priority SA" (LoD No. 7448 filed by pltf.). 

46. On 23-11-2017, the plaintiff's lawyer in Sudan Mr. Elie Medlej e-mailed to the plaintiff's representative, stating inter alia, "Dear Stavros, I have been chasing the Sudanese lawyers and I received a brief reply to all our queries: —The adjournment of the auction will be made on the basis of objections to be filed with the Court of Appeal in Port Sudan against the decisions made. The grounds of such objections is the lack of authority of the Master, the abuse of trust by him, the initiation of arbitration in London, the injunction in Panama and the non-notification to the owners. The Court might postpone the Court sale after the second hearing prior to 17th December 2017. The lawyers will file the objections on Monday" (LoD No. 7508 filed by pltf.). 

47. Apart from the question of the validity of the arbitration clause after expiry of a period of 12 months from the date of completion of discharge at Port Sudan, or cancellation or non-performance of the contract, suffice it to say that, there is no evidence that the arbitration proceedings commenced in London. The arbitration clause No. 17 does not oust the jurisdiction of the Court of Sudan or of any Court. The cause of action arose within the jurisdiction of Sudan. Therefore, the Court of Sudan proceeded with the case having jurisdiction and was competent to adjudicate the same (Canada Shipping and Trading SA vs TT Katikaayu and arm, 54 DLR 93, Admiralty Court of Bangladesh). 

Injunction in Panama and plaintiff's conduct: 
48. It is stated at para 8 of the plaint that earlier on 29-4-2016, the First Maritime Court of Panama, upon the application of Monjasa A/S, passed order No. 130 (Case No. 40608-2016) issuing a general protective measure against the vessel in order to prevent the registration of any act implying the transfer, sale, alienation or cancellation of the vessel from the Panamanian Registry. It appears from the LoD No. 10437 dated 3-12-2025 filed by the plaintiff that the injunction/prohibition order was lifted in 2022. The order dated 29-4-2016, passed in Panama, does not, by any means, oust the jurisdiction of the Sudanese Court and the competency of the Sudanese Court cannot be called in question. 

49. It is further stated at para 19 of the plaint that the plaintiff, being unaware of the judicial sale of the vessel in Sudan, entered into a Memorandum of Agreement to sell the vessel to a third party for USD 2.93 million with a delivery schedule between 20-3-2018 and 10-4-2018. The parties, as I understand, were unable to close the deal for obvious reasons. 

50. The above-stated facts unequivocally show that the plaintiff has not come with clean hands and they attempted to twist and frustrate the judicial sale in Sudan having full and up to date knowledge about the proceedings in Sudan Court. 

Bonafide purchaser for value; registra-tion/deregistration etc. The Acrux (No. 2): 51. In support of Mr. Rahman's argument that the defendant No. 2B is not a bonafide purchaser and has not obtained a clean title, it is stated in the plaint that there is a missing link between the auction purchaser and the defendant No. 2B as to the transfer of ownership of the vessel. The subsequent transfer and/or chain of title involving defendant No. 2A (Kokusai Transport) and defendant No. 2B is tainted with fraud and illegality in that they are sister companies sharing same ultimate beneficial owner (Asnim Wardono) and director (Andre Astono). Therefore, the sale from Kokusai to the defendant No. 2B was not an arm's-length transaction. Kokusai's knowledge is imputed to defendant No. 2B. On 2-3-2018 (three days prior to the 4th and final auction), Kokusai offered USD 3 million to the plaintiff to purchase the vessel. 

52. It is further stated that the purported subsequent owner failed to obtain a deletion certificate of the vessel from the Panamanian Registry; that the vessel was subsequently registered in the Cook Islands and then deregistered in July 2018 due to irregularities following communication between Cook Islands and the plaintiff; the Memorandum of Agreement between Kokusai and defendant No. 2B dated 7-9-2018 falsely represented the vessel's flag as "Cook Islands" despite the prior deregistration; and, that the vessel was then fraudulently shown registered in Zanzibar/ Tanzania in October, 2018 but the Zanzibar registry was officially closed at that time and registration of foreign owned vessels would have been impossible. 

53. Mr. Rahman argues that the above-stated facts establish that the defendant No. 2B has failed to establish mandatory requirement that their ownership is rooted in judicial sale and that they have a clean chain of title as was held in Rich Step Shipping vs MV Ocean Dawning. 

54. It is true that in the reported case, the Appellate Division endorsed the finding of fact of the Admiralty Court that the subsequent purchaser satisfied the Court about the entire chain of its purchase of the vessels. A close reading of the judgment shows that the observation as to the subsequent purchaser's clean chain of title was a mere statement of fact, it was not a question of law. The question of law was whether the judicial sale in North Korea conferred clean title upon the first instance purchaser. The answer was 'yes' and the original registered owner lost the case. The clean chain of title of the subsequent purchaser in the reported case reinforced the purchaser's case, but that was not the factor in reaching the decision. 

55. In the case in hand, with regard to the question as to the failure of the subsequent purchaser to obtain a deletion certificate from Panama, registration in Cook Islands and deregistration in July, 2018, then registration in Zanzibar/Tanzania in October, 2018 etc., The Acrux (No. 2) is recalled. Suffice it to say that the question is whether the judicial sale is Sudan was conclusive. The answer is 'yes'. It follows that the plaintiff has lost their title in the vessel and they cannot question the subsequent events in regard to the validity of the ownership of the subsequent purchasers or deregistration, registration etc. of the vessel. The plaintiff does not have any locus standi to raise these issues. They are now third parties, their only interest and right lie in the sale proceeds deposited in the Sudanese Court/ treasury. 

Order: 
For the reasons stated above, the application for vacating the order for arrest is allowed. The order for arrest dated 4-8-2025 is hereby recalled and vacated. Let the vessel MV DK 03 (IMO No. 9082908) be released at once provided the same is not arrested in connection with any other suit/case. Marshal of the Court shall execute the release order at the costs of defendant No. 2B. 

End.

full_judgment:
Yousuf Abdullah Suman, J: In this writ petition the petitioner, Unique Cement Industries Limited, prayed for a direction upon the respondent nos.1 and 2, Bangladesh Bank, under sections 45 and 49 of the Bank Companies Act 1991 to direct the respondent nos.4 & 5, Islami Bank Bangladesh Limited, for encashment of a Bank Guarantee issued by Islami Bank on behalf of the respondent no.6, M/s Rabeya Traders, in favour of the instant petitioner- the beneficiary of the said Bank Guarantee, and a Rule Nisi was issued to that effect by this Division on 08.04.2018. 

2. The facts of the case in brief are that, the petitioner is a cement producing and selling company carrying its business at home and abroad through dealership. The respondent no.6, M/s Rabeya Traders, obtained such dealership from the petitioner, and as a condition under the dealership, the respondent no.6 submitted a Bank Guarantee being no.12 dated 19.04.2015 for an amount of TK.50,000,00/ (fifty lakh) issued by the respondent nos.4 & 5 Bank in favour of the petitioner which was valid for one year till 18.04.2016 (Annexure-A to the writ petition). The respondent no.6 subsequently failed, as claimed by the petitioner, to pay the dues to the petitioner, and the petitioner hence made a demand to the respondent nos.4 & 5 Bank for encashment of the said Bank Guarantee on 20.12.2015 within its validity period (Annexure- H to the Supplementary Affidavit). A few days later on 29.12.2015, in furtherance to a purported negotiation between the parties, the petitioner placed a revised demand to the respondent nos.4 & 5 Bank in place of its original Bank Guarantee of fifty lakh (Annexure- L-3 to the Affidavit-in-Opposition filed by the respondent nos.4 & 5). The negotiations failed. The respondent nos.4 & 5 Bank, however, did not encash the said Bank Guarantee in favour of the petitioner. A few days later, the respondent no.6 instituted a suit being Title Suit No.1 of 2016 in the learned Joint District Judge Court, 1st Court, Rajbari praying for an injunction upon the encashment of the said Bank Guarantee on 10.01.2016. The prayer was rejected. Being aggrieved by, the respondent no.6 filed a First Miscellaneous Appeal being Civil Rule No.08 (FM) of 2016 (arising out of FMAT No.19 of 2016) in this Division and obtained an order of injunction on 18.01.2016 upon the encashment of the said Bank Guarantee (Annexure- I to the Supplementary Affidavit). The petitioner’s second demand for encashment of the said Bank Guarantee dated 21.01.2016 was thus rejected by the respondent nos.4 & 5 Bank on the ground of this order of injunction on 27.01.2016. The said Bank Guarantee was expired on 18.04.2016. The aforesaid Title Suit No.1 of 2016 of the learned Joint District Judge Court, 1st Court, Rajbari was, however, withdrawn by the respondent no.6 on 25.04.2016. The aforesaid FMAT No.19 of 2016 was also dismissed by this Division as being not pressed and the connected Rule was discharged resulting in the order of injunction vacated on 03.05.2016. The respondent nos.4 & 5 Bank, however, refused to encash the said Bank Guarantee, at this time, on the ground of its being expired, and cancelled the said Bank Guarantee on 09.05.2016. The respondent no.6 filed another civil suit being no.55 of 2016 on 09.08.2016 for declaration of the demand for encashment of said Bank Guarantee illegal even after cancellation of the same by the respondent nos.4 & 5 Bank on 09.05.2016 – the latest position of which is unfounded in records. The petitioner therefore made two representations on 19.06.2016 and 19.09.2016 to the respondent nos.1 & 2, Bangladesh Bank, praying for a direction upon the respondent nos.4 & 5 Bank, for encashment of the said Bank Guarantee in favour of the petitioner vide Annexure-C and F to the writ petition respectively. The respondent nos.1 & 2, however, failed to take any effective move for encashment of the said Bank Guarantee till date. Hence the case. 

3. Mr. Murad Reza, the learned senior counsel appearing for the petitioner, submits that, the petitioner placed the demand for encashment of the said Bank Guarantee No.12 dated 19.04.2015 in time on 20.12.2015 whereas the expiry date was on 18.04.2016; and when a Bank Guarantee is placed in time for encashment, the issuing bank has no legal right to refuse payment unless they have an issue of fraud. He refers Uttara Bank vs. Macneil and Kilburn [1981] 33 DLR (AD) 298 wherein it was held that “the contract to pay to the seller is absolutely obligatory. No direction upon the bank to withhold payment can be passed – only exception is in case of fraud of which the bank has notice”. As to the order of injunction on the said Bank Guarantee granted by this Division, the learned senior counsel submits that, the decision is erroneous and conflicting to the settled principles of law established by our jurisdiction as was held in Nuvista Pharma vs. NBR [2013] 65 DLR (AD) 302 that “injunction on the Bank Guarantee cannot sustain in view of the decision of the case of Uttara Bank vs. Macneil and Kilburn reported in 33 DLR (AD) 298 wherein it has been held that there cannot be any injunction whatsoever upon any Bank Guarantee”. He further submits that respondent nos.1 & 2, Bangladesh Bank, has statutory duties to direct the respondent nos.4 & 5, Islami Bank Bangladesh Limited, for encashment of the said Bank Guarantee in favour of the petitioner under Section 45 and 49 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991. In relation to this, he refers the cases of ASF Rahman vs. Bangladesh Bank [2000] 52 DLR (AD) 61, JIT Knit Composite vs. Government of Bangladesh [2013] 18 BLC 480, Delta Spinners vs. Bangladesh Bank [2015] 20 BLC 339 wherein it has consistently been held that the Bank Companies Act, 1991 clearly invest Bangladesh Bank with a strong regulatory power over the functioning and business of banking companies. In addition, he refers the ICC Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantee (URDG 758) and submits that the instant Bank Guarantee comes within the purview of Article 2 of the same which defines a ‘Guarantee’ as any signed undertaking, however named or described, providing for payment on presentation of a complying demand. The learned senior counsel therefore prays for the Rule to be absolute. 

4. Mr. S M Tariqul Islam, the learned senior counsel appearing for the respondent nos.4 & 5 Bank, on the other hand, submits that, though the petitioner placed its first demand in time on 20.12.2015 for encashment of the said Bank Guarantee, 9 (nine) days later it submitted another revised demand on 29.12.2015 requesting to issue a new Bank Guarantee for 25 (twenty five) lakh and a payment order for 19 (nineteen) lakh in place of the encashment of the original Bank Guarantee of 50 (fifty) lakh (Annexure- L3 to the Affidavit-in-Opposition filed by the respondent nos.4 & 5). He therefore suggested a negotiation between the parties as to the payment dues under the Bank Guarantee, and submitted that the petitioner itself prevented the instant respondents for not making the payment under the said Bank Guarantee vide Annexure-L3, mentioned above, adding that the petitioner never submitted the original Bank Guarantee to them while requesting for its encashment. He further submits that, on 18.01.2016 this Division granted an order of injunction upon the encashment of the said Bank Guarantee and hence the respondent nos.4 & 5 Bank could not make the payment. The Guarantee however expired on 18.04.2016 during the order of injunction being in force. The respondent nos.4 & 5 Bank therefore could not encash the said Bank Guarantee during its validity period, and after its expiry the respondents had no other options but to cancel the said Bank Guarantee and they did so on 9.5.2016, he submits. The learned senior counsel finally submits that, this case is burdened by disputed question of facts and therefore not maintainable in writ jurisdiction. 

5. Learned counsel Mr. Syed Hasan Zobair appeared for the respondent nos.1 & 2, Bangladesh Bank. Filing an affidavit in opposition, the learned counsel submits that, since the matter was subjudice due to the order of injunction granted by this Division, Bangladesh Bank had no scope to give any decisions during the period of injunction. Subsequently on 01.08.2016, after the expiry of the period of said order of injunction, the bank, however, instructed the respondent nos.4 & 5 Bank to take effective initiatives to resolve the matter in issue vide Annexure-D to the writ petition. He therefore submits that, Bangladesh Bank has discharged its duty under the law, and thus the Rule be discharged as having no merit. The learned counsel, however, also submitted that, the respondent Bangladesh Bank would remain abide by the verdict of this Hon’ble Court. In addition, upon a query made by this Court, he asserted that a Bank Guarantee is payable immediately. 

6. Learned Deputy Attorney General, Mr. Dihider Masum Kabir, also placed a written submission before us arguing that the cancellation of Bank Guarantee by Islami Bank is unlawful, and that a bank guarantee must be honoured if presented in due time for encashment unless any fraud or misrepresentation is found. Learned DAG therefore submits that Islami Bank misused their powers with malafide intention and as such a direction may be given to Bangladesh Bank to settle the issue as per law, i.e., under section 45 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991. 

7. We have gone through the writ petition as well as the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner, two affidavits in oppositions filed by the respondent nos. 1 & 2 - Bangladesh Bank, and the respondent nos. 4 & 5 – Islami Bank Bangladesh, and also two written submissions placed before us by the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Deputy Attorney General. We have also given our anxious consideration to the submissions made by all the parties involved herein. 

8. It is admitted that the demand for encashment of the Bank Guarantee being no.12 dated 19.04.2015 for an amount of TK.50,000,00/ (fifty lakh) was placed by the petitioner before the issuing bank, Islami Bank Bangladesh Limited, in time on 20.12.2015 whereas the expiry date was 18.04.2016 (Annexure-L to the Affidavit in Opposition filed by the respondent nos.4 & 5). Islami Bank, the respondent nos.4 & 5, received this letter of demand on 24.12.2015 requesting them to encash the said Bank Guarantee within 7 (seven) days from the date of its receipt. 5 (five) days thereafter on 29.12.2015, Islami Bank received a revised demand in place of the original Bank Guarantee of 50 (fifty) lakh. The fresh demand, however, maintained a reservation clause stating “This is without any prejudice to our encashment letter mentioned above” i.e., the original demand letter dated 20.12.2015 (Annexure-L3 to the Affidavit in Opposition filed by the respondent nos.4 & 5). The original demand therefore remains valid for all material time. The order of injunction was granted on 18.01.2016. The respondent nos.4 & 5 Bank thus had around 28 (twenty eight) days in hands to honour the said Bank Guarantee before the order of injunction was granted- whereas a Bank Guarantee is payable on demand. Clause (1) of the said Bank Guarantee reads as follows: “1. To make unconditional payment of Tk.50,00,000/- (Fifty lac) only to you & your demand without any question and without any reference whatsoever of our client.” 

9. As to the issue of granting injunction by this Division upon the encashment of the said Bank Guarantee, we find that this decision of granting injunction is not compatible with the settled principles as to the granting of injunction upon Letter of Credits and/or Bank Guarantees consistently followed by our apex court in a number of cases, including, Uttara Bank vs. Macneil and Kilburn [1981] 33 DLR (AD) 298, Smart Apparels vs. Hanvit Bank Kuni Bong Branch [2005] 57 DLR (AD) 194, Nuvista Pharma vs. NBR [2013] 65 DLR (AD) 302. In Nuvista Pharma, referred above, it was held that, “injunction on the Bank Guarantee cannot sustain in view of the decision of the case of Uttara Bank vs. Macneil and Kilburn reported in 33 DLR (AD) 298 wherein it has been held that there cannot be any injunction whatsoever upon any Bank Guarantee”. Recently a larger Bench of this Division followed the same principles in First Miscellaneous Appeal No.242 of 2021 with Civil Rule No.202 (FM) of 2021 in an unreported case of Meejab Limited vs. AA Knitspin Limited decided on 16.07.2024. We are therefore of the view that the decision of granting injunction by this Division was not an informed decision. 

10. As to the issue of disputes and negotiations between the petitioner and the respondent no.6- the supplier and customer respectively- raised and suggested by the learned counsel appearing for the respondent nos.4 & 5, we hold that in Edward Engineering vs. Barclays Bank [1978] LLR Vol.1. 166, referred and approved by our apex court in Uttara Bank vs. Macneil and Kilburn, referred above, Lord Denning M.R. observed that, “It is not concerned in the least with the relations between the supplier and customer; nor with the question whether the supplier has performed his contractual obligation or not; nor with the question whether the supplier is in default or not. The bank must pay according to its guarantee, on demand, if so stipulated, without proof or conditions. The only exception is when there is a clear fraud of which the bank has notice”. It is nobody’s case herein that there is any fraud of which the bank got notice. Further, if the customer, respondent no.6 herein, has any grievances in law the same can be remedied by bringing an appropriate action for compensations or damages. In the light of the above, we do not find any reason as to why Islami Bank Bangladesh, the respondent nos.4 & 5, shall be entitled to refuse the payment under the said Bank Guarantee. 

11. Now, whether Bangladesh Bank, the respondent nos.1 & 2, have authority to give directions upon the respondent nos.4 & 5, Islami Bank, for encashment of the said Bank Guarantee in favour of the petitioner under Section 45 and 49 of the Bank Companies Act, 1991? The relevant parts of these two sections are reproduced herein below. 
45. Power of Bangladesh Bank to give directions 
(1) If Bangladesh Bank is satisfied to the effect that- 
(Ka) … 
(Kha) … 
(Ga) for preventing activities detrimental to the interest of the depositors of any bank company or prejudicial to the interest of the bank company; or 
(Gha) for securing the proper management of any bank company, it is necessary to issue directions to the bank companies generally or to any bank company in particular, it may issue such directions as it deems fit; and the bank company concerned shall be bound to comply with such direction. 
49. Further powers and functions of Bangladesh Bank 
(1) Bangladesh Bank may- 
(Ka) … 
(Kha) require bank companies generally or any bank company in particular, to refrain from taking any specific action in relation to any particular matter concerning their or its business, or to take such action in relation thereto;
It is evident from the above referred text that Bangladesh Bank has sufficient authority to give mandatory directions upon the bank companies under Section 45, and under Section 49 it has power to issue directions both in the nature of prohibition and mandamus. 

12. Further, in ASF Rahman vs. Bangladesh Bank [2000] 52 DLR (AD) 61, B B Roy Choudhury, J held that, “Section 45(1)(Ga)(Gha) and section 49(Kha) of the Bank Companies Act clearly invest Bangladesh Bank with a strong regulatory power over the functioning and business of banking companies”. This decision has been followed in JIT Knit Composite vs. Government of Bangladesh [2013] 18 BLC 480 with the following findings: “we are of the view that the ends of justice would be best served if a direction has been [is] given upon the respondent no.2, Bangladesh Bank to give a decision upon the application dated 22.07.2012 (Annexure-L) filed by the petitioner positively in terms of sections 45(1)(Ga)(Gha) and 49(Kha) of the Bank Companies Act, 1991”. In addition, in Delta Spinners vs. Bangladesh Bank [2015] 20 BLC 339, it was held that “it has now become the obligation of the Bangladesh Bank to take appropriate actions against concerned L/C issuing banks for their illegal role in stopping re-imbursement against those L/C”. 

13. Thus, the law and the corresponding judicial rulings confirm that Bangladesh Bank has sufficient authority, if not a duty or obligation, to give directions upon bank companies generally or to any bank company in particular. 

14. In addition, under Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees (URGD 758) issued by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), the instant Bank Guarantee is in alignment with the demand guarantee defined in Article 2 of the ICC URGD 758. Further, under Article 16 of Uniform Customs and Practice (UCP 600) a bank under the law and banking practice is bound to make payment or re-imbursement in respect of the accepted bill once they are accepted by the issuing banks, and once such acceptance is given, the matter is closed and the concerned banks are precluded from raising any issue thereafter (Delta Spinners vs. Bangladesh Bank, referred above). 

15. In the light of the above findings and observations we conclude that (a) that the said Bank Guarantee was placed for encashment on time; (b) that the injunction granted by this Division upon the encashment of the Bank Guarantee was not an informed decision and thus susceptible to the settled principles consistently followed by our apex court; (c) that the issues of disputes as to the performance of obligations under the guarantee between the contracting parties are hereby set to naught; aggrieved party’s grievances can be remedied by bringing an appropriate action for damages; (d) that performance of guarantee, letter of guarantee, letter of credit, documentary credit, bank guarantee, etc., are of cognate; (e) that Bangladesh Bank has sufficient authority, if not a duty or obligations, to give direction upon the bank companies under the law; and (f) that the international commercial practices are also in alignment with the observation we made above. 

16. Premised in the above, this Court finds merit in the application and the substance in the Rule issued. 

17. In the result, the Rule is made absolute with the following direction. 

18. The respondent nos.1 & 2, Bangladesh Bank, are hereby directed to take effective and efficient action in order for encashment of the Bank Guarantee being no.12 dated 19.04.2015 for an amount of TK.50,000,00/ (fifty lakh) issued by the respondent nos.4 and 5, Islami Bank Bangladesh Limited, on behalf of the respondent no.6, M/s Rabeya Traders, in favour of the petitioner, Unique Cement Industries Limited, within 30 (thirty) days from the date of receipt of a copy of this judgment and order.

There is no order as to costs.

Communicate this judgment and order at once.

End.

Mazharul Islam (Md) ------- Petitioner
VS
Dr. Mohammad Abdus Salam and others ------- Respondent-contemners.
case_source: (Arising out of Writ Petition No. 2424 of 1995).
full_judgment:
Farah Mahbub, J: On the allegation of authoring, publishing and disseminating contemptuous statements in the article in question authored by the contemner-respondent No.1 under the caption "ফিরে দেখা বিচার বিভাগ পৃথকিকরণ” in the "Daily Jugantor" dated 1-11-2024, a contempt Rule was issued by this Court upon the respective contemner-respondents with direction to give reply with affidavit-in-connection with the article, published in the said newspaper on 1-11-2024. In compliance thereof the contemner-respondent No.1, the author of the said article, filed affidavit-of-compliance on 10-11-2024. However, upon tendering unconditional apology it has been stated therein that he would not contest the contempt Rule being full of remorse and contrition. By filing a supplementary affidavit contemner-respondent No.1 further stated that meanwhile the publication of the Article "ফিরে দেখা বিচার বিভাগ পৃথকিকরণ” in the "Daily Jugantor", authored by him, had been withdrawn on 23-11-2024 (Annexure-1). More so, the Editor and the Publisher also expressed their regret by publishing a rejoinder in the said newspaper on the same date. 

2. Subsequently, the contemner-respondent No.1 by publishing a separate rejoinder, published in the respective newspaper on 03-12-2024 (Annexure-2), filed another supplementary affidavit, annexing the said rejoinder, reiterating the statements that the article in question authored by him has been withdrawn and at the same time the Editor, the Publisher including the Author expressed their regret in the said rejoinder. 

3. Today, when the matter has been taken up for hearing the contemner-respondent No.1, at the outset, tenders unconditional apology and throws himself at the mercy of this Court for commission of the inadvertent mistake causing contempt of this Court while authoring the said Article and expresses deep sorrow, repentance and remorse for the same. In this regard, his further assertion is that the article in question was written in connection with the judgment and order passed in Writ Petition No. 2424 of 1995 followed by Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.79 of 1999 analyzing the subject matter of the issue, i.e. separation of judiciary in the context of its execution against the public perception, not to undermine the judiciary and this Hon'ble Court. 

4. He further goes to assert that the background context which led the contemner to author the article is that while he was functioning as 1st Class Magistrate in Bagura District in 1999, he recorded some confessional statements of the accused under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in Sessions Case No.113 of 2000, pending in the Court of learned Additional Sessions Judge, 2nd Court, Bagura. After about 24 years of recording the said confessional statement the contemner, who has meanwhile retired, was called for, to give his depositions in respect of recording those statements. However, for travelling from Dhaka to Bogura, for attending the court for recording his deposition he will not get any TA/DA; thus, causing serious hardship for a retired person like him. However, he realized that the Article in question might have caused uncalled for mischief and he regrets for it. 

5. He also averred that there was no wilful negligence on his part in respect of authoring the article. Accordingly, he seeks unconditional apology for causing disrespect to this Hon'ble Court and commits that he will never pen such an article which will undermine the prestige and dignity of the judiciary. Hence, for the cause of justice he may be exonerated from the contempt proceeding. 

6. In support, the contemner respondent No.3 also filed an affidavit-of-compliance stating, inter alia, that the contemner respondent No.1 has already given a rejoinder with regard to the article wherein he clearly stated that he regretted the mistakes being committed by him while writing the article in connection with the interpretation of the judgment of the apex court passed in the case of Masdar Hossain vs Secretary, Ministry of Law Justice & Parliamentary Affairs and others, and sought for unconditional apology. 

7. In this regard, the respondent-contemnor Nos.2 and 3 in their rejoinder, published in the respective newspaper, have also sought for unconditional apology for publishing such sensitive article and both the rejoinders, seeking unconditional apologies, have been published in the "Daily Jugantor" on 23-11-2024 and 24-11-2024 respectively. Further, it has been asserted therein that the contemners do firmly believe in the supremacy of the judiciary. They also believe for effective separation of the judiciary from the executive, necessity to have separate Secretariat and to have separate financial arrangement so that the judiciary can run its function independently without any dependency on the other organs of the State. Also, "Daily Jugantor" has always been in support towards enforcement of the judgment of Masdar Hossain Case. 

8. Under the circumstances, the contemners again offer unconditional apology for their unintentional and bonafide mistake in publishing the article in question touching the issues of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh as well as the judiciary and, as such, prayed for exonerating them from the charge of contempt of court upon accepting their unconditional apology, for the cause of justice. 

9. Later, by publishing another rejoinder on 01-12-2024 (Annexure-2) in the "Daily Jugantor" the contemners respondent Nos.2 and 3 reiterated their earlier assertions and upon annexing the said publication filed affidavit-of-compliance afresh before this Court on 02-12-2024. 

10. Per contra, the categorical contention of the petitioner is that while discussing the limits of criticism of a judge or court, the Hon'ble Appellate Division in State vs Swadesh Roy, "Daily Janakantha", 68 DLR (AD) 162 held that the criticism of a judge or court must be fair and an improper imputation amounts to contempt of court. In this regard, the following observation is notable. 
"Scandalization, to express shortly, includes an attack upon any Judge in his public capacity for, such attack would be calculated to malign the judge and to lower the authority of the Court over which the judge performs his judicial function. At the same time, it also amounts to interference with the course of justice and the proper administration thereof. Criticism of judges of the highest Court in respect of acts done in their administrative capacity, which contain improper imputation, amounts to contempt. If the Chief Justice is criticized for acts done in his administrative capacity this" also amounts to contempt. The criticism should be fair and not made with oblique motive or with the object of maligning the justice delivery system and lowering the majesty of the law and dignity of the Court in the estimation of the public." 

11. With regard to the Supreme Court's power to give punishment for contempt of court, the Appellate Division in the above-mentioned decision, further observed as follows: 
"The expression used in Article 108 is extensive in nature. The framers of the Constitution intended that the Supreme Court should have power to punish for contempt of itself only by inserting the expression 'to make an order for the investigation of or punishment for any contempt of itself". This provision confers upon the apex court the power to punish for contempt of itself and in addition, it confers some additional power relating to contempt as it appears from the expression 'including'. This expression has been used in a wider scope of power, that is to say, this Court has the power to punish the contempt of itself and also something else, which could fall within the inherent jurisdiction of the court of record." 

12. Accordingly, it has been contended that this Hon'ble Court is at liberty to apply its discretion on whether or not to accept what is claimed to be an "unconditional apology" and also to determine whether an apology tendered before it is, in fact, a remorseful and unconditional apology. 

13. In this regard, Mr. Tanim Husain Shawon, the learned Advocate for the petitioner relying upon the decision of the case of State vs Advocate Md. Quamrul Islam MP and others, 25 BLT (AD) (2017) 83 : 22 BLC (AD) 90, submits that in the said case though the contemners tendered "unconditional apology", the Hon'ble Appellate Division imposed a fine. Referring to the context of the present case, he submits that the impugned Article titled "ফিরে দেখা বিচার বিভাগ পৃথকিকরণ”, published in the. "Daily Jugantor" on 01-11-2024, exceeded all limits of fairness, inasmuch as it contained deliberate misrepresentation of the judgment of the Hon'ble Appellate Division in the Masdar Hossain Case; it contained improper imputation on the judges who passed the judgments in the said case; it was a clearly calculated attempt to instigate, tension between the judiciary and the other organs of the State; and the publication was deliberately timed so that the ongoing reform initiatives to fully implement the independence of the judiciary in the light of the judgment of the said case was disrupted. 

14. More so, he goes to contend, the affidavit dated 24-11-2024 filed by the contemner-respondent No.1, annexing an alleged retraction published on 23-11-2024, does not exhibit a proper remorse on the part of the said contemner, inasmuch as he has sought to justify the article, published on 01-11-2024, without admitting that he misrepresented the judgment of the Hon'ble Court in the Masdar Hossain Case and also, that he made improper imputation on the judges concerned. The contemner tendered a perfunctory apology merely for the use of some words and sentences in the article, which not only underplays the extent of the contemptuous aspects of his article but is also tantamount to a tactic to avoid the consequences of the offence of criminal contempt of court, perpetrated by him. 

15. In addition, he submits, at paragraph No. 9 of his affidavit, the contemner-respondent No. 1 has narrated a "background context" for publishing his article which clearly has no nexus or relevance to the contents of the article. As such, the statements in the aforesaid paragraph demonstrate a complete lack of remorse on the part of the contemner. 

16. Accordingly, he prays for making the Rule absolute with imposition of necessary punishment upon the contemners. 

17. In view of the above context, we have perused the affidavits of compliance of the respective contemner respondents along with the supplementary affidavit offering unconditional apology with a prayer for exonerating them from the charge of contempt of court. We have also examined the rejoinders dated 23-11-2024, 01-12-2024 and 03-12-2024 respectively seeking unconditional apology to the public at large for authority, publishing and disseminating the contemptuous statements in the article in question. 

18. The fundamental right of freedom of speech and expression, as contained in Article 39(2) of the Constitution, is subject to the reasonable restriction or the limitation on the scope of reporting of a judicial proceeding or any stage thereof. However, "fair criticism" or "comment" on the merit of any case which has been heard and finally decided, will not render the person concerned guilty of contempt of court. 

19. The classic exposition of the right of criticism is that of Lord Atkin when he said: 
"The path of criticism is a public way; the wrong headed are permitted to err therein; provided that members of the public abstain from imputing improper motives to those taking part in the administration of justice, and are genuinely exercising a right of criticism, and not acting in malice or attempting to impair the administration of justice, they are immune. Justice is not a cloistered virtue: she must be allowed to suffer the scrutiny and respectful, even though outspoken, comments of ordinary men.": 
Ambard vs Attorney-General of Trinidad: AIR 1936 PC 141. 

20. Quoting the above passage the Supreme Court of India observed in Rama Dayal Markarha vs State of Madhya Pradesh : AIR 1978 SC 921, p-927, 
"Fair and reasonable criticism of a judgment which is a public document or which is a public act of a Judge concerned with administration of justice would not constitute contempt. In fact, such fair and reasonable criticism must be encouraged because after all no one, much less Judges, can claim infallibility. A fair and reasonable comment would even be helpful to the Judge concerned because he will be able to see his own shortcomings, limitations or imperfection in his work. The society at large is interested in the administration of public justice because in the words of Benjamin Cardozo, 'the great tides and currents which engulf the rest of men do not turn aside in their course and pass the Judges by.' Such permissible criticism would itself provide a sensible answer to sometimes ill-informed criticism of Judges as living in ivory towers. But then the criticism has to be fair and reasonable……. 
If the criticism is likely to interfere with due administration of justice or undermine the confidence which the public rightly repose in the courts of law as courts of justice, the criticism would cease to be fair and reasonable criticism as contemplated by section 5 but would scandalise courts and substantially interfere with administration of justice." 

21. Also, Sawant J, speaking for the Supreme Court in Re: Sanjiv Datta, underscored the principles of fair comment and criticism on constitutional fundamentals. 
"The responsibility to maintain the rule of law lies on all individuals and institution. Much more so on the three organs of the State. Our Constitution has separated and demarcated the functions of the Legislature, the Executive and the judiciary. Each has to perform the functions entrusted to it and respect the functioning of the others………  
The Constitution entrusts the task of interpreting and administering the law to the judiciary whose view on the subject is made legally final and binding on all till it is changed by a higher court or by a permissible legislative measure. Those living and functioning under the constitution have to accept and submit to this obligation of respecting the constitutional authority of the courts. Under a constitutional Government, such final authority has to vest in some institution. Otherwise, there will be a chaos. The court's verdict has to be respected not necessarily by the authority of its reason but always by reason of its authority. Any conduct designed to or suggestive of challenging this crucial balance of power devised by the Constitution is an attempt to subvert the rule of law and an invitation to anarchy." 

22. There is no clear cut test formulated by the courts to find out whether a particular criticism can be branded as a "fair comment". Though fair criticism, if made in good faith, works as a defence to contempt but it limited its availability depending on surrounding circumstances, i.e. the person making the comments,.his special knowledge in the field of comments and the purpose sought to be achieved: Arundhati Roy, Re, A 2002 SC 1375, 1394 : (2002) 3 SCC 343. 

23. However, when from the criticism a deliberate, motivated and calculated attempt is discernible to bring down the image of.. judiciary in the estimation of the public or to impair the administration of justice or tend to bring the administration of justice into disrepute the courts must bitter themselves to uphold their dignity and the majesty of law: Ajay Kumar Pandey, JT 1998(6) SC 571: (1998) 7 SCC 248. 

24. It is apparent on a fair reading of the article, titled "ফিরে দেখা বিচার বিভাগ পৃথকিকরণ”, published in the "Daily Jugantor" on 01-11-2024, that there was misrepresentation of the judgment of the Hon'ble Appellate Division passed in Masdar Hossain Case. Said article poses question on the exercise of jurisdiction of the Court who passed the said judgment with a view to have an independent separate judiciary and to uphold justice and rule of law. Above all, the Article has been published at such a juncture when reform initiatives are in progress towards independence of judiciary in the light of Masdar Hossain Case. Resultantly, it undermines the object of passing the judgment in question for an independent judiciary, to achieve maintenance of purity in the administration of justice. 

25. In this regard, it is pertinent to note that before any news or articles are published on any judgment passed by the court of law or on the function of judicial administration, concerned quarters/authority, i.e. the Editor, who controls the selection of the matter which is to be published in a particular issue of the newspaper, and the Publisher, who is responsible for publication, must ensure that the statements/comments so made are not distorted, to be careful its attributing motives, its objective approach and analysis. After all, "the court's verdict has to be respected not necessarily by the authority of its reason but always by reason of its authority." 

26. From the affidavit-of-compliance, it does not appear that the respondent Nos.2 and 3 made any assessment to that effect prior to selection for publication of the said article in the respective newspaper. 

27. However, fact remains, subsequent to publication of the article in question in the newspaper on 01-11-2024 they published rejoinders on two occasions seeking unconditional apology before the public at large. 

28. We, however, accept the unconditional apology offered by the contemner-respondent Nos. 2 and 3 taking into consideration of the 2nd rejoinder published in the respective newspaper on 01-12-2024 (Annexure-2 of the affidavit-of-compliance dated 02-12-2024) and also, considering the commitment so made by them to remain cautious and careful in future while editing and publishing any article which will have an adverse impact on the administration of justice in the estimation of public at large. Consequently, they are exonerated from the charge of contempt of court.
 
29. However, contemner-respondent No.1, the author of the article, has also sought for unconditional apology to this Court by filing affidavit-of-compliance and also, by publishing rejoinders in the newspaper twice, one, on 23-11-2024 and another, on 03-12-2024 seeking apology before the public at large along with the withdrawal of the said publication from the respective newspaper. 

30. Considering the above, we accept his unconditional apology and thereby exonerating him from the charge of contempt of this Court with caution to remain extremely careful from now on while writing any article which may create any misconception in the administration of justice and also, in the estimation of public at large. 

31. With the above observation this Rule is accordingly disposed of without any order as to costs. 

Communicate the judgment and order to the respondents concerned at once. 

End.
